title: Fitbit Data Can Finally Sync to Apple Health
content:
The latest update to the Google Health app for iOS allows Google Health data to sync to Apple Health. Google's app is used to collect data from wearables like Fitbit trackers and the Pixel Watch.


Sync to Apple Health. Share your data like your exercise records, sleep, vitals, steps, and more from Google Health to Apple Health.

Google Health (previously the Fitbit app) collects fitness, sleep, and wellness data from a connected wearable device. Steps, distance traveled, heart rate, sleep, and more can now be added to Apple Health. As noted on Reddit, some data such as HRV doesn't transfer over.

Syncing can be enabled after downloading the update by selecting Connections, choosing Apps and services, and then adding Apple Health.

Apple Health data already synced to Google Health, so the new update adds two-way sync between the platforms. Fitbit devices have never had native sync to Apple Health, and users previously had to use a third-party syncing utility or a workaround to transfer data.

available from the App Store for free. The update also adds Smart Health Links for sharing medical records with providers or family members.

title: Apple faces new antitrust case in Russia over state-backed apps
content:
Russia has escalated its long-running dispute with Apple by opening an antitrust case that could cost the iPhone maker nearly $50 million over its refusal to preload state-backed apps.


Russia opens antitrust case against Apple over iPhone apps
After years of threatening to do so, Russia has finally begun investigating Apple after it failed to preinstall state-backed apps onto devices in the country. The apps in question are Max, a state-backed messaging service, and RuStore, a domestic app store.
"The company did not comply with the FAS warning to preinstall the national messaging app and the national app store on its iOS devices (iPhone, iPad). The FAS opened a case against the company in accordance with the competition law and the already established law-enforcement practice in regard to Apple," a statement seen by Interfax said.

title: Report: Apple aiming to launch camera-equipped AirPods this fall
content:
Macworld


We’ve been reporting on Apple’s plan to stick cameras on AirPods Pro since summer 2024, believe it or not. It was supposed to happen earlier, but setbacks in Apple Intelligence and Siri delayed them, just like Siri delayed Apple’s new HomePod mini and its push into the smart home market.
Now, according to a brief update in Mark Gurman’s Power On newsletter at Bloomberg, they could finally be on the way this fall alongside Apple’s other smart home products.
Gurman says the original camera-equipped AirPods were developed under the codename B798. Apple frequently develops multiple competing versions of the same product, and in this case, one of the alternative designs was codenamed B790. This B790 version, Gurman reports, appears to be further along, with the code name already referenced in the OS 27 betas and a scheduled launch as early as this fall, barring any further delays.
What are camera-equipped AirPods?
The AirPods-with-cameras have been rumored long enough that we sort of expected them to be the AirPods Pro 3. We got a heart rate sensor instead, along with some battery life and audio improvements.
Supposedly, the AirPods with cameras are said to resemble AirPods Pro 3, and it’s not yet known if they will include a heart rate sensor or not. It’s also not known what the name will be: AirPods Pro 4, AirPods Ultra, or something else entirely.
The cameras are said to see both standard spectrum and infrared, but reportedly won’t be used for taking photos and videos—the quality and placement would be poor for that. Instead, the cameras are meant to be used for AI-powered features. That could be recognizing your hands for gesture controls, adjusting audio based on the environment, or recognizing if someone is talking to you or just talking nearby. It could also be used to give Siri a set of “eyes” where the AI assistant can give you answers that are appropriate for the context of your current surroundings and activity as part of Visual Intelligence.
There are lots of other possibilities for AirPods with cameras that would necessitate changes to other Apple software and services, too. Think of workout tracking that can count reps and sets when you lift weights, or nutrition tracking based on ingredient labels or analyzing what’s on your plate. Currently, there’s no information to suggest any specific use case for the camera-equipped AirPods, but there are lots of possibilities, now and in the future.

title: Apple's iCloud File Sharing Left Ex-Employees With Access to Secret Documents
content:
The way Apple combines work and personal iCloud accounts left some employees able to access confidential documents after departing the company, reports The Information. The site spoke to more than half a dozen former Apple employees who were unknowingly left with access to sensitive content.


The former employees said many Apple files they had been shared on over their careers at the company—including planning documents for product launch events—continued to sync to their personal devices through the iCloud storage service after they left Apple. In some cases, they even received notifications about fresh updates to the documents. Some former employees said they were petrified to delete the files for fear that doing so would attract Apple's attention.

Apple files get mixed in with employees' accounts because the company encourages them to use their personal Apple Accounts with their work ‌iCloud‌ account. Employees are given a 2TB ‌iCloud‌ plan and are able to merge the storage with their existing Apple Account or create a new account. Since only one primary account can be signed in at a time, most opt to use their existing account to avoid having to carry two iPhones.

Apple has a managed folder for workplace files that it revokes access to when an employee leaves, but some internal documents aren't saved there automatically and shared files end up mixed in with personal content. Employees can also retain access to iMessage chats and files shared via the Messages app.

In its filing, Apple alleged that former employee Chang Liu breached Apple's systems using a "rare, previously unknown authentication bug" to download files while he was working at OpenAI.

The Information that the OpenAI lawsuit is unrelated to any files left available on ‌iCloud‌ and that it does not pursue legal claims against former employees who accidentally have Apple documents in their personal ‌iCloud‌ accounts.
This case is about OpenAI employees wrongfully taking Apple's secret and confidential information regarding our unreleased technologies, processes, and products. Nothing in the filing relates to documents shared by, or stored in, iCloud.

Former employees say Apple does not do a thorough enough job going through personal devices to remove sensitive files that have been stored in ‌iCloud‌. In a now-settled legal dispute, chip company Rivos claimed Apple intentionally lets former employees retain access to files "as part of a planned effort to generate a pretextual basis to sue the employees and their new employer for 'stealing' Apple material." In the Rivos case, an employee was targeted for keeping work files in his personal ‌iCloud‌ account.

Another former Apple employee sued by Apple, Gerard Williams, countersued and accused the company of using intimidation tactics to scare people thinking of leaving. Apple sued Williams for breach of contract after he started processor company Nuvia, presenting extensive phone and text records of his communications. The court rejected Williams' claim, and Apple dropped the case in 2023.

also accused former Vision Pro engineer Di Liu of downloading thousands of corporate documents to his personal cloud storage shortly before leaving the company for Snap.

The Information does not outright suggest Apple is purposefully allowing former employees to retain access to ‌iCloud‌ files, but points out that Apple's use of ‌iCloud‌ for file sharing and its incomplete wiping of employee accounts are at odds with its heavy focus on privacy and security.

title: If you want a MacBook Air, you should buy one ASAP
content:
Macworld


First it was the Mac mini. Then the Mac Studio. Now, the memory crisis is aiming to wipe out stock of yet another Mac, this one far more popular.
If you’re looking to buy a MacBook Air, it might be hard to find one before the end of August. As we saw with the Mac mini earlier this year, delivery estimates on Apple.com are beginning to show delays as Apple scrambles to get more stock.
As reported by Mark Gurman in his latest Power On newsletter, the seemingly minor delay on Apple.com—orders are currently shipping with a two-week backlog—is indicative of a much larger issue caused by memory shortages. Gurman reports that Apple is scrambling to keep new MacBooks in stock during the back-to-school and upcoming holiday shopping seasons by sourcing RAM from China and “prominently steering customers toward the base MacBook Pro,” which starts at $1,999, several hundred dollars more than the $1,299 Air.
Upselling is a tactic Apple rarely deploys at its stores, and it could backfire. Apple has built a ton of trust with consumers over the years by largely letting buyers dictate the budget they want to spend, whether that means an iPad, iMac, or MacBook. Coupled with price hikes that are still fresh in people’s minds, steering consumers into higher-end products they don’t need could cross the line from sensible to sleazy.
Apple isn’t expected to update the MacBook Air with an M6 processor until spring 2027, though it’s unclear whether that will fix the issue. The M6 MacBook Air is expected to use the same LPDDR5X RAM as the current model, and there are no signs that the supply issues will ease before 2028. In its recent financial results conference call, Tim Cook reiterated that Apple is facing “a hundred-year flood on the memory pricing” and is “evaluating all options” to balance costs and supply.
On Monday morning, Amazon still had the 13-inch MacBook Air in stock for $1,243, about $50 less than the Apple Store, which was quoting an August 18-25 delivery window. Also reader David points out that Apple’s refurbished store has several in stock as well for $200 less than you’d pay for a new one. Apple refurbs come with a full 1-year warranty and go through a “rigorous” inspection process.
But whichever model you choose, you should probably act fast.

title: Best Games for Mac 2026: A-list Mac games to play
content:
Macworld


For years, gaming on a Mac meant compromises: fewer releases, weaker performance, and the quiet assumption that serious players needed a Windows PC. That’s no longer entirely true.
Thanks to Apple silicon, improved developer support, and a growing number of high-quality ports, there are now genuinely great games that run well on macOS. Not just indie experiments or casual time-killers, but full-scale RPGs, strategy games, and visually demanding titles that take advantage of modern Mac hardware.
This list focuses on the best Mac games you can play right now, not everything that technically runs on macOS. Every game here was chosen based on performance on Apple silicon, quality of the Mac version, and whether it’s actually worth your time and money. We’ve also excluded games that rely heavily on emulation or feel meaningfully worse than their Windows counterparts.
Mac gaming still isn’t perfect, but if you own a recent Mac, it’s better than it’s ever been. These are the games that prove it. 
Best Mac Games to play in 2026
There are so many great games available to play on the Mac. Everyone has different tastes though, so we’ve tried to include something for everyone below. So whether you love RPGs, fighting games, action-adventure, first-person shooters, strategy games or puzzle, read on to find something to play.
Below you can find the best games released in 2025, plus the ones we loved and will continue to play in 2026. Updated August 2026 to add our reviews of Total War: Attila and Age of Empires II: Definitive Edition.

More than 25 years after the original game first appeared on Mac, Age of Empires II: Definitive Edition has finally arrived as a native macOS release thanks to Feral Interactive. While it has taken an extraordinarily long time to get here, the wait has been worthwhile. This remastered version updates one of the greatest real-time strategy (RTS) games ever made with sharper high-resolution graphics, bundled expansion content and Apple Silicon support, making it feel at home on modern Macs.
The game spans roughly a thousand years of history, from the Dark Ages through the Medieval era, allowing players to command dozens of civilizations in campaigns inspired by real historical figures such as Joan of Arc, Attila the Hun and Vlad Dracula. The Definitive Edition includes the original game alongside three DLC expansions, dramatically increasing the amount of content with additional civilizations, maps and historical campaigns. Combined with skirmishes and replayable scenarios, there are hundreds of hours of strategy gameplay available.
Gameplay remains as compelling as ever. Players must gather resources, expand settlements, research technologies and build armies while responding to enemy attacks in real time. Although experienced strategy fans will quickly feel at home, the game also includes excellent tutorials that teach both basic mechanics and more advanced tactical concepts, making it approachable for newcomers.
The Mac version does have a few drawbacks. It only supports Apple Silicon Macs, leaving older Intel machines behind. Multiplayer is also restricted to Mac users, so there is no cross-platform play with Windows players. In addition, the interface occasionally shows its age, and the game does a poor job of explaining that the enhanced graphics pack requires a separate free download after installation.
Fortunately, these issues do little to diminish what is still one of the finest RTS games ever created. The updated visuals preserve the charm of the original while making battles look crisp on modern displays, and the sheer volume of campaigns and historical scenarios provides outstanding value for money.
For Mac owners who enjoy strategy games, Age of Empires II: Definitive Edition is an easy recommendation. It successfully modernises a timeless classic without losing the gameplay that made it legendary, proving that great strategy games never go out of style.

Total War: Attila was originally launched for Intel Macs and PCs way back in 2015 – when the macOS was still called OS X. Needless to say, changes to both Apple’s hardware and operating systems meant that the Mac version fell by the wayside several years ago, but Feral Interactive has now brought the game back to the Mac, providing native support for current Apple Silicon Macs, and Apple’s Metal graphics system (although it no longer runs on Intel Macs anymore, unfortunately). At the moment, the game is currently only available on Steam – and requires macOS 15.7 or later to run – although Feral tells us that it will be released on the Mac App Store later this year.
 Following on from last year’s Total War: Rome, the action this time around moves forward to 370AD as the now faltering Roman Empire has split into two rival factions and finds itself under attack on all fronts. There’s a prologue section that begins with the Battle Of Olbia, which acts as a tutorial for new players as well as setting the historical context for the campaign ahead of you. When you’re ready, you can begin the main campaign by taking control of any of the various factions within the game. You can command the Eastern Roman Empire, the Saxons of the Barbarian Kingdoms, or the Sassanids of the Persian Eastern Empire. But, of course, the star of the show is Jason Momoa – aka the beardy warlord Attila, who leads the fearsome hordes of the Hun.
 In previous Total War games you had to build up your forces by methodically gathering resources, such as wood, stone and gold, which then allowed you to train your troops and develop new weapons. However, the Hun tribes are nomadic, so instead of settling in a specific region and quietly developing towns and cities, the Huns charge across Europe on horseback, raiding the lands of their enemies to gain wealth and resources. This makes for a more dynamic playing style where you can throw caution to the winds and unleash the Huns to swarm across Europe, wreaking havoc left, right and center. You can hit the ground running and start raiding and pillaging right from the start of the campaign, giving Total War: Attila a more ‘invade first, ask questions later’ style of play than other games in the series.
 The age of the game also means that you don’t need a high-end Mac to run it properly. We had no problems running it on a MacBook Pro with an M2 processor, and the game’s graphics settings provide presets that are suitable for a wide range of Mac models. Once the main campaign is complete you can buy a number of expansion packs that extend the campaign further, or test yourself by recreating a number of great historical battles or setting up your own custom battles against computer-controlled opponents. There’s an online multiplayer mode as well although – as with many Mac games – you are limited to playing only with other Mac players.

Slay the Spire 2 is a confident sequel that builds on one of the most successful deck-building games available on Mac. Rather than dramatically changing the formula, developer Mega Crit focuses on refining what made the original so addictive, introducing a host of small improvements, more content and a new cooperative multiplayer mode. The result is a game that feels familiar but remains fresh enough to justify the sequel.
The core gameplay remains unchanged. Players battle their way up a mysterious spire by choosing different routes through a map of rooms, fighting monsters, collecting new cards and relics, and making strategic decisions about how to strengthen their deck. As a roguelike, every defeat sends you back to the beginning, encouraging experimentation and rewarding players who learn how different cards and abilities work together. The game remains easy to pick up but offers plenty of depth for players willing to master its systems.
While the sequel doesn’t reinvent the experience, it adds considerably more variety. Returning characters are joined by two new classes, the Necrobinder and the Regent, each bringing fresh abilities and play styles. There are more skills, relics and rare cards to discover, along with new quests and encounters that encourage players to rethink their route through each run. Daily challenges and custom game modes also return, while the headline new feature is a co-op mode for up to four players, allowing friends to tackle the Spire together for the first time.
Our main criticism is the presentation. Although the 2D graphics have been improved, the visuals remain fairly basic, lacking the atmosphere and visual flair found in some rival games. However, those simple graphics also help the game run smoothly on both Intel and Apple Silicon Macs, making it accessible to a wide range of hardware.
Overall, Slay the Spire 2 is an excellent sequel. It may not introduce many major new ideas, but its numerous refinements, additional content and enjoyable co-op mode make it a must-have for fans of the original. Newcomers, however, may want to start with the first game before moving on to the sequel.

Why we loved Blue Prince: Blue Prince is one of the most inventive puzzle-adventure games in years, blending roguelike mechanics with atmospheric mystery in a way that feels both fresh and deeply satisfying. Its constantly shifting mansion keeps you thinking strategically and creatively, while its layered secrets reward curiosity. 
Blue Prince is an indie puzzle-adventure that updates the feel of classic exploration games with slick 3D visuals and a mystery-driven structure that’s perfect for Mac players. In the game you’re Simon P. Jones, heir to the mysterious Mt. Holly mansion, and your only path to inheriting the estate is to locate the elusive “Room 46.” To do that you explore a sprawling 45-room mansion where the layout changes every in-game day, forcing you to rethink your approach constantly.
As you wander from room to room, you choose which spaces to open next, building out your blueprint while managing a limited number of steps. Some rooms contain useful items that grant extra movement, while others offer clues tied to deeper mysteries hidden in the mansion. Because the mansion resets each night, planning ahead and taking careful notes becomes a strategic part of the experience, giving the game the feel of a mystery you’re slowly unraveling over many sessions.
Visually, Blue Prince blends hand-drawn charm with true 3D exploration, creating a warm but curious atmosphere that suits its puzzle focus. The pacing is unhurried; it favors thoughtful investigation over action, so it’s well suited to fans of cerebral, methodical games rather than fast-paced thrills.
Overall, Blue Prince will likely appeal most to players who enjoy deep mystery, clever puzzles, and the satisfaction of piece-by-piece discovery. Its blend of adventure, strategy, and roguelike resets makes it an engaging experience for curious players on macOS.

Why we loved Cyberpunk 2077: Cyberpunk 2077 (Ultimate Edition) nailed the comeback. The vast, neon-soaked world of Night City offers deep freedom, compelling characters and quests, and slick futuristic visuals. After many patches (and expansion Phantom Liberty), it plays smoothly even on Macs – making the once-troubled RPG feel “alive” and worth exploring.
Cyberpunk 2077, despite its troubled 2020 launch, sold more than 30 million copies. Now CD Projekt Red has made Cyberpunk: 2077 available for the Mac—on the App Store, Steam, and Epic Games Store.
The game is set in the Blade Runner-inspired Night City, a megalopolis obsessed with power, glamour, and body modification. 
Initially, the first-person viewpoint suggests a straightforward FPS, but it’s actually a deep and challenging role-playing game that boldly steps into the future, avoiding tired fantasy clichés. 
Your character – who can be male or female – is a hacker known as V, and you start the game by choosing one of three ‘lifepaths’ that fill in V’s background. You can assign experience points to attributes such as intelligence, reflexes, technical ability and ‘cool’, with each attribute giving you access to different skills that you can develop throughout the game. And, of course, there are plenty of body modifications and upgrades that you can collect along the way too. 
V is sent on a mission to steal a prototype chip called the Relic, but then ends up with the Relic implanted inside their own head. Death Stranding, the idiosyncratic and sometimes downright bizarre game from Hideo Kojima, the renowned developer behind the long-running Metal Gear series, arrived on the Mac in 2024.
The game is set in a near-future version of the United States, in the aftermath of a mysterious apocalyptic event known as the Death Stranding, which has caused the collapse of society. All that’s left are a few scattered communities, which rely on ‘porters’ to deliver supplies and help set up a communications system called the Chiral network. That’s where you come in, playing Sam ‘Porter’ Bridges – who is voiced by, and modeled on the actor Norman Reedus of Walking Dead fame – as he trudges across the country delivering his supplies. Along the way, you’ll encounter terrorists and creepy invisible monsters called BTs (‘beached things’), but your real foe for much of the game is simply the environment around you.
There is some combat in Death Stranding, but your main task as a porter is to struggle across the rocky, ruinous countryside as you embark on a series of missions to deliver your cargo of medicines and other supplies. The game is sometimes described as a ‘walking simulator ’ as you spend much of your time clambering over rocks, up hills, or wading across rushing rivers and streams. That may not sound terribly exciting, but there’s a lot of satisfaction as you struggle to slowly inch your way towards the peak of a craggy hill with your cargo intact.
The game also has a dramatic cinematic flair – possibly a little too cinematic, as the first 45 minutes or so is really just a series of very long cut-scenes, interspersed only by a few brief sequences where you learn how to control Sam as he walks, jumps and wades across the rocky terrain. The long cut-scenes can try your patience in the early stages of the game, but they do look terrific – the landscapes have a cinematic scope, and the 3D graphics are tremendously detailed and realistic. And the feeling that this is the gaming equivalent of a blockbuster Hollywood production is further emphasized by cameos from a number of other Hollywood big names, including Mads Mikkelsen, Guillermo Del Toro, and Lindsay Wagner.

You might need an M2 or M3 to really enjoy the game’s sweeping vistas and eerie special effects, but seeing a game like Death Stranding running on an M1 iMac gives us some hope for the future of games on the Mac.

What is the best way to run a PC game on a Mac
The best way to run a PC game on a Mac depends on the game itself and your hardware, but the options generally fall into three categories: native Mac ports, compatibility layers, and virtual machines. Here’s a breakdown of the most effective approaches.
Native Mac Ports: The simplest and most reliable way to play a PC game on a Mac is to choose titles that have been natively ported to macOS. All the games we have reviewed above run natively on macOS. This avoids the performance penalties of emulation or translation layers. 
Many major titles now ship with native Apple Silicon support, including Cyberpunk 2077 Ultimate Edition, Civilization VII, Frostpunk 2, and Assassin’s Creed Shadows.
Key consideration: Native ports are the best option when available, but the library is still smaller than Windows. Most native Mac games require Apple Silicon (M1 or newer) and at least 16GB of RAM for demanding titles. 
Compatibility Layers (CrossOver / Game Porting Toolkit): For Windows-only games that lack a Mac port, compatibility layers are the next best option. CodeWeavers CrossOver is the leading commercial solution. As described in our Best Virtual Machine Software for Mac guide, CrossOver translates Windows API calls into macOS equivalents, allowing many Windows apps and games to run natively rather than through a virtual machine. CrossOver offers a polished consumer-friendly interface with regular updates that improve compatibility with popular titles like Diablo IV and Path of Exile 2. It doesn’t require a Windows license, making it lighter and more affordable than a full VM.
Key consideration: Compatibility is still the biggest limitation – not every Windows game works, and performance can vary. 
Virtual Machines (Parallels Desktop, VMware Fusion): Virtual machines let you run a full copy of Windows alongside macOS, which can be useful for games that don’t work through compatibility layers. However, this approach carries a significant performance overhead because the game is running through both a hypervisor and the Windows emulation layer. That’s why CrossOver is generally preferred for gaming because it avoids the overhead of a full VM.
Parallels Desktop and VMware Fusion are the top VM options, but they require a Windows license and are best suited for older or less demanding games. 
Key consideration: VMs are generally the slowest option for gaming and should be considered a last resort for demanding titles.

 FAQ 


1.
How Apple has made Macs better for gaming
Apple has introduced several software features to bridge the performance gap. Here are some of the technologies designed to maximize hardware efficiency. 
MetalFX Frame Interpolation & Denoising: Part of the Metal 4 API, these features use AI to generate extra frames and improve lighting effects like real-time path tracing.
Game Mode: This feature prioritizes gaming tasks on the CPU and GPU while reducing latency for wireless controllers and AirPods.
Game Porting Toolkit 2: This free set of tools created by Apple helps developers bring Windows games to Mac faster, supporting advanced features like Ray Tracing on M3 and M4 chips
Dedicated Games App: macOS Tahoe introduces a centralized hub for tracking achievements, friends, and launching titles from the App Store or Apple Arcade.





2.
Do these games run natively on macOS, or do they require emulation?
All of the games included in this list run natively on macOS. We’ve avoided titles that rely primarily on emulation or compatibility layers because that often leads to performance issues and inconsistent long-term support.





3.
What’s the minimum Mac I need to play these games?
The games on this list require M1 Mac or newer. More demanding titles benefit from 16GB of RAM and a Pro or Max chip, but many will still run well on base-model MacBooks with adjusted settings.





4.
Are Mac versions missing features compared to Windows versions?
Unfortunately it is a fact that some ports lag behind Windows in updates or mod support, but for most players the core experience is the same. We call out meaningful differences in our reviews when they affect gameplay or value.





5.
Is it better to buy games on Steam or the Mac App Store?
Steam may offer incentives, such as sales prices and easier access to updates and mods. The Mac App Store is convenient and tightly integrated with macOS, but it can be more expensive and slower to receive updates.





6.
Do these games support controllers on Mac?
Many do. PlayStation and Xbox controllers work well on macOS, though some games still play best with keyboard and mouse. We note controller support in individual game entries where it matters.





7.
Will these games work on future versions of macOS?
Games with active developer support are far more likely to remain compatible with future macOS updates. 





8.
Do I need to change settings to get good performance?
Often, yes. Even on Apple silicon Macs, lowering resolution or graphics settings can significantly improve frame rates. Most of the games here offer flexible options that let you balance visuals and performance.





9.
Is the MacBook Airs good enough for gaming?
Surprisingly, yes, but within limits. Base-model MacBook Airs can handle many of these games well, especially turn-based and indie titles. Sustained performance may drop during long sessions due to passive cooling, but casual and moderate gaming is very feasible.





10.
Why aren’t more big AAA games on Mac?
Game development is still heavily centered on Windows and consoles, and macOS remains a smaller market. That’s slowly changing as Apple silicon matures, but Mac gaming still relies on selective ports rather than simultaneous releases.





11.
Can I use Apple’s Game Porting Toolkit to play games on my Mac? 
The Game Porting Toolkit isn’t a consumer product, but some Mac enthusiasts have discovered that it can also be used to run many Windows games directly on macOS. However, tools like CrossOver are a much easier to use solution for playing PC games on a Mac. For games developers the GPTK is a useful tool for optimizing Windows games for the Mac.

title: Ted Lasso is here to shake up Apple’s quiet August–but big things are on the way
content:
Macworld


Ever since Apple pulled out of Macworld New York back in 2023, August is traditionally a pretty slow month for Apple releases, but it’s a big one for the Apple rumor mill.
We don’t expect any new hardware this month with the looming iPhone/Apple Watch event coming in September. If you like your surprises spoiled, though, August is a good month for Apple rumors. Production will kick up for the new iPhones and Apple Watches, and sometimes other hardware that Apple plans to release in the fall. And with large-scale manufacturing comes leaks. 
So August will probably be the month we get our best picture of the upcoming iPhones, Macs, and other devices Apple has planned for release this fall. Plus, the new operating systems are well into their public beta testing process—those will continue, but there probably won’t be any big surprises.
This will be Tim Cook’s last month as CEO, as John Ternus will take over the role on September 1. Oh, and Ted Lasso is back!
OS 27 beta testing continues
We don’t expect any new hardware in August (not with the big September iPhone event so close), but there will be plenty of software to check out if you participate in the beta program.
We’re currently at the fourth beta release for all the OS 27 updates: iOS, macOS, iPadOS, watchOS, visionOS. New releases go out to developers every two weeks or so, with the public beta testers getting the same builds a day or two later. So expect two more beta releases in August, potentially three.
At this point, most of the big features and changes in the OS 27 betas are already here, and Apple is just refining things, fixing bugs, and optimizing performance. We’ll be scouring the builds for potential hidden information about the upcoming products, too.

title: Apple Launches New Legal Challenge Against UK Backdoor Demand
content:
Apple last month filed a new legal complaint with the UK's Investigatory Powers Tribunal (IPT) over the British government's demand for access to encrypted iCloud backups belonging to UK users, according to an order issued by the court and reported by the Financial Times.


The Home Office previously agreed to drop its original demand for a backdoor covering UK and U.S. customers alike, after a diplomatic row with Washington. The British government subsequently issued a new technical capability notice (TCN) to Apple last year, limited to users in the UK.

Technical capability notices are issued under the UK's Investigatory Powers Act, which the government says is necessary to investigate terrorism and child sexual abuse. They can force companies to hand UK security services access to customer data, even when that data is encrypted.

separate complaint against such notices at the IPT, with that case due to be heard in December.

title: iPhone price hikes are coming: ‘Absolutely no doubt’
content:
Macworld


When Apple hiked prices last month, one notable product that was spared from the sticker shock was the iPhone. All seven of the iPhone models Apple currently sells, including the two-year-old iPhone 16 and 16 Plus, have the same starting prices as before: $599 for the iPhone 17e, increasing incrementally all the way up to the $1,199 Phone 17 Pro Max.
In just a few weeks, that’s likely to change. After hearing reports for months that the iPhone 18 Pro will come with a price hike this fall, Mark Gurman weighs in with a comment in his latest Power On Newsletter. In no uncertain terms, he says prices will be going up on iPhones this fall. The only question is, how much.
In a response to a reader question about iPhone prices, Gurman says in plain language: “There is absolutely no doubt that Apple will raise iPhone prices, for a variety of reasons.” Chief among them, of course, is the current memory supply crunch that has affected the entire industry and is largely responsible for Apple’s recent Mac and iPad price hikes. But Gurman also says the new camera system in the iPhone 18 Pro, which is expected to have a variable-aperture lens, is also pricier than the current model.
It’s notable that the price of Apple’s high-end iPhone hasn’t really changed much over the past decade. When Apple introduced the iPhone X in 2017 with a $999 price tag, it set a new standard for flagship phones. However, the iPhone 17 Pro, which is most comparable to that model, costs just $100 more, starting at $1,099. Granted, the larger iPhone 17 Pro Max pushes it even higher, with storage options all the way up to $1,999, but iPhone prices have remained remarkably stable for a while, even with bigger screens, more and better cameras, and higher-end components.
As far as the extent of the hikes, Gurman is somewhat unclear, though he says “the iPad and Mac increases in recent weeks have given us a bit of a road map.” Therefore, he expects $100-$200 price increases, and a starting price for the folding iPhone Ultra of “at least $2,000, if not more.” Less clear is whether Apple will adjust the prices of the standard iPhone 17 and 17e, which aren’t expected to get updates until next spring.

content:

Our Verdict 
CrossOver is a WINE-based compatibility layer that runs many Windows apps and games on a Mac without Windows. It’s ideal for gamers and older software, but compatibility varies. Apple Silicon Macs currently require Rosetta to run CodeWeavers.

Best for: Mac gamers who want to avoid buying Windows and for running older Windows apps.
Not for: Users who need guaranteed compatibility and Apple Silicon users who want fully native performance – at the moment CrossOver requires Rosetta to work on Apple Silicon and some apps don’t work. CodeWeavers has announced that CrossOver 27, when it launches, will address this issue. 
CrossOver is a commercial version of the open-source WINE compatibility layer that lets you run many Windows applications and games on a Mac without installing Windows or buying a Windows licence. Rather than virtualising Windows like Parallels Desktop or VMware Fusion, it translates Windows API calls into macOS equivalents, making it a lighter and often less expensive alternative. See how CrossOver compares to other Mac Virtual Machines we have tested in: Best Virtual Machine for Mac.
WINE itself is free but can be difficult for non-technical users to configure. CodeWeavers developed CrossOver to provide a more user-friendly experience, complete with technical support and tools that simplify installing Windows software and games.
CrossOver is particularly well suited to Mac gamers and anyone who needs to run older Windows software. However, compatibility isn’t guaranteed, and some applications won’t run at all. Current versions also rely on Apple’s Rosetta translation layer on Apple Silicon Macs, although CrossOver 27 is expected to add native Apple Silicon support. Before buying, it’s worth using the 14-day free trial to make sure your essential apps and games work as expected.
This review was updated in August 2026 to take account of the new versions CrossOver 26.1 and 26.3. 
How well does CrossOver perform
At the moment, CrossOver is based on code that was originally written for Intel processors, so it relies on Apple’s Rosetta to run on Macs with Apple Silicon, but performance is still pretty good, and CodeWeavers states that it is working on native support for Apple Silicon coming in CodeWeavers 27 in early 2027.
How easy is it to use CrossOver
CrossOver has always aimed to be more user-friendly than WINE, by allowing you to install Windows apps into ‘bottles’ – which are self-contained files that can be launched and run on your Mac without requiring a full copy of Windows. You can create lots of different bottles for different apps, and bottles can even be configured to provide compatibility with different versions of Windows. This is useful as it allows you to create bottles that are suitable for older games and software that might require a particular version of Windows in order to run properly.
Even so, CrossOver can still be quite complicated at times, so back in 2022 CodeWeavers introduced a new interface that was redesigned to be more Mac-like, and also to provide more help when installing many Windows apps and games. When you launch CrossOver you see the main Install window, which lists some popular Windows apps and games, such as The Witcher 3 and Diablo IV, and even productivity tools such as the Quicken accounting software for business users.

				
					

				
			
Playing Diablo in Full Screen

Foundry




There’s also a search tool that provides information on hundreds of other Windows apps, and an indication of how well they run with CrossOver. But, as we discovered, there are degrees of compatibility here, with some apps that run well, while others may run with problems – and some may simply not work with CrossOver at all. But, somewhat to my surprise, I was able to install and run a 20-year old copy of Microsoft Publisher from an old DVD with no trouble at all, and also Icewind Dale II, an old favourite of mine that doesn’t seem to be widely available these days.

				
					

				
			
Find an app to install

Foundry




Which Windows apps and games work with CrossOver?
CrossOver supports hundreds of Windows applications and games, with one of the broadest compatibility libraries available for macOS. While it works with productivity software such as Quicken and many older Windows applications, gaming is its main focus. Apple’s Game Porting Toolkit is built on open-source CodeWeavers technology, and the company regularly releases updates that improve compatibility with the latest PC games.
Recent releases have added or improved support for titles including Diablo IV, Diablo II: Resurrected, Overwatch, Path of Exile 2, Dragon’s Dogma 2, Fallout 76, Kingdom Come: Deliverance II, The Outer Worlds 2 and Clair Obscur: Expedition 33. 

				
					

				
			
Diablo running in a window
.
Foundry




However, compatibility isn’t universal: some apps and games run perfectly, others have minor issues, and some won’t run at all. Before buying, you can search CodeWeavers’ online compatibility database to check whether the software or games you need are supported.
What’s coming in CrossOver 27?
CrossOver 27 is expected to be one of the biggest updates yet when it arrives in early 2027. Current versions are written to run on Intel-based Macs and still rely on Apple’s Rosetta translation layer to run on Macs with Apple Silicon processors, but Apple is planning to retire Rosetta with macOS 27 Golden Gate, coming later in 2026. 
CodeWeavers has confirmed that CrossOver 27 will run natively on Apple Silicon. This should deliver better performance while allowing CodeWeavers to modernise the interface and add features that weren’t possible while supporting Intel Macs.
The downside is that CrossOver 27 will no longer support Intel-based Macs. However, existing Intel users can continue using older versions of CrossOver instead of upgrading.
Latest CrossOver updates
CrossOver continues to receive regular updates, many of which focus on improving support for specific Windows games. CrossOver 26 was released in February 2026. The 26.1 update came in April 2026. The current version is CrossOver 26.3, which arrived on July 21, 2026. 
What’s new in CrossOver 26.1: More game support 
CrossOver 26.1 might not seem like a major update, but it will be big news for many Mac gamers. Diablo IV and Overwatch are two hugely popular games from Blizzard that don’t run natively on the Mac, and have also proved stubbornly resistant to CodeWeavers’ attempts to get them running on the Mac via CrossOver. Thankfully, CrossOver 26.1 seems to have solved that problem – as long as you’re running macOS Tahoe 26.5 on your Mac.
At long last, we were able to get Diablo IV running on our MacBook Pro with an M2 Pro chip, and it managed a smoothly playable 50fps when set at 1920×1080 resolution and medium graphics settings. There are still a few rough edges – we had some problems with the cursor and window sizes when the MacBook was connected to an external monitor, but it only took a little trial and error to find settings that worked for our set-up. The CrossOver 26.3 update in July 2026 brought bug fixes that resolve issues for Diablo IV, the Epic Games Launcher, and GOG. 
CodeWeavers also states that Diablo II: Resurrected will run with Tahoe 26.5 as well, although it’s still working to fix a bug that can cause the game to crash if you use Command-Tab to cycle through open applications on your Mac while you’re playing. 
As always, there’s a 14-day trial available so that you can see how well your favourite Windows games work with CrossOver before buying.
What’s new in CrossOver 26: Technical updates 
Whilst there aren’t many major new features, this update does provide numerous technical updates that focus on improving performance for running Windows apps – and games in particular.
Core engine update: As we’ve mentioned, CrossOver is based on the open-source WINE software, which allows Windows apps and games to run on macOS as well as other Linux-based operating systems. CrossOver 26 now adopts the latest Wine 11.0, which, according to the developers at CodeWeavers, introduces more than 6,000 technical improvements, and fixes hundreds of bugs. 
Gaming and graphics: Apple makes a contribution too, as its Game Porting Toolkit (GPT) – which uses open-source elements taken from both WINE and CrossOver – also includes a feature developed by Apple itself, called D3DMetal. This is designed to improve compatibility between games that use the Windows D3D graphics system and Apple’s own Metal graphics software, and CrossOver 26 now supports the latest version of D3DMetal 3.0, which should help to improve compatibility and graphics performance with many Windows games. 
Interface changes: There are also some interface updates in CrossOver 26 to help it work more smoothly with the Liquid Glass interface in macOS Tahoe. And, of course, there are some fixes for a number of popular games that may not have worked well with CrossOver in the past. These include recent, big-name titles such as Kingdom Come: Deliverance II, The Outer Worlds 2 and – right at the top of my own gaming wishlist – the multi-award-winning Clair Obscur: Expedition 33.
What was new in CrossOver 25: Streamlined installation 
The March 2025 launch of CrossOver 25 was one of the biggest updates of recent years, with CrossOver promising to bring “next level gaming to the Mac”. 
Core engine update: Some of the new features in v25 were under-the-bonnet changes, such as adopting the latest version of the underlying WINE technology, which CodeWeavers claims includes thousands of programming updates to improve performance and compatibility. 
Gaming and graphics: This update also introduced a new graphics technology, called DXMT that, according to CodeWeavers, provides better performance for less powerful Mac models when running Windows games that use DX11 graphics. The update added improved compatibility with lots of big-name Windows games, allowing you to play games such as Path Of Exile 2, Dragon’s Dogma 2, and Fallout 76 for the first time. And, along with Steam, CrossOver 25 now supports the Windows versions of the GoG and Epic game stores so that you can download games that you own from those stores.
Installation process improvements: CodeWeavers also continues to further streamline the installation process for Windows games and apps for new users who may not have a lot of technical experience. As well as providing a list of popular games and other apps that work well with CrossOver, this new version now has the ability to connect to the compatibility database stored on the CodeWeavers website, and can automatically apply the best graphics and audio settings for a variety of different games.
CrossOver Price: How much is CrossOver?
That technical support means that CrossOver isn’t free, costing $74/£60 for a license that provides 12 months of technical support and updates, or you can pay $494/£414 for CrossOver Life, for lifetime support.
However, there’s a 14-day free trial available, so that you can see if it works with the Windows software and games that you want to run before buying (and there’s also a version of CrossOver available for Linux as well).
Should you buy CodeWeavers CrossOver?
The sheer effort that the CodeWeavers team puts into providing regular updates for CrossOver is impressive, and we’ve had good experiences using their tech support to get help running the Windows version of Steam on our ageing office iMac. Even so, CrossOver can still be rather complicated for new users, so it’s definitely worth downloading the trial version to see how well it works with your favourite Windows games and other Windows software.

title: Apple's Smart Glasses Could Become Its Next Health Device
content:
Apple wants its future glasses and headsets to double as health and fitness devices, Bloomberg's Mark Gurman reports.


In the latest edition of his "Power On" newsletter, Gurman said the ambition traces back to Vision Pro's early development, when Apple weighed a number of ambitious health and fitness features for the headset. Among the ideas Apple explored was a Vision Pro-native take on Fitness+, designed to have wearers work out and follow along with classes while the headset's body-tracking sensors monitored their form. That project stalled and was ultimately scrapped, according to Gurman, both because of technical limitations and because the headset was simply too heavy to wear comfortably during a workout.

AirPods, which Apple transformed from simple earbuds into a functioning hearing aid system. Sensors embedded in the glasses, he suggested, could eventually let Apple capture movement data in a similar way, opening the door to fitness-tracking functionality later down the line.

debut next year; he expects the health capabilities to arrive gradually, over a period of years rather than at launch.

He pointed out that the Vision Products Group, Apple's team responsible for glasses and future headsets, is looking to hire a "strategic product design leader" tasked with helping "define the future of health, well-being and fitness experiences across vision products." Whoever fills the role will need to "translate ambiguous opportunities at the intersection of spatial computing, wearables, consumer health and human behavior" into an actual product direction.

The listing also calls for a candidate with "experience developing and validating digital health or fitness products" and "familiarity with sensor-driven experiences." Put together, Gurman argues, the posting confirms Apple's intent to eventually place its glasses alongside AirPods and Apple Watch as health platforms.

title: Best Virtual Machine Software for Mac (2026): Compare Parallels, VMware Fusion, UTM & more
content:
Macworld


Even the most loyal Mac users recognize that Windows still rules the roost in the world of desktop and laptop computers, and there are many important apps that only run on Windows. For example, the Windows version of Microsoft Office includes the Access database that has never been available for the Mac, and there are many professional graphics and video tools that are Windows-only. And, of course, there are all those A-List games that have never even glanced in the direction of us poor, forgotten Mac gamers.
If you need to run Windows software or games on your Macs then this article will reveal the best way to do so. 
Read on to discover the best options for running Windows, and Windows apps, on your Mac. You may also like to read our guide to How to install Windows and run Windows apps on a Mac (M-series models). We also cover how to run Windows on an Intel Mac separately.
Best Virtual Machine for Mac 2026: Best VMs to run Windows on a Mac
Read on for the best virtual machines for Mac. Our top choice is Parallels, but we also consider VMware and alternative options, including emulators that let you run Windows apps on a Mac without even installing Windows to Microsoft’s Windows 365 service.

Parallels Desktop is the best virtual machine for Mac users who need to run Windows, Linux or another copy of macOS alongside macOS. It creates a virtual PC on your Mac, allowing you to run Windows applications without rebooting or partitioning your drive.
One of Parallels’ biggest strengths is its seamless integration with macOS. You can keep Windows and macOS completely separate or use Coherence mode, which lets Windows apps run alongside Mac apps as if they were native. You can even pin Windows applications to the Dock, while shared folders, drag-and-drop and copy-and-paste make moving between the two operating systems effortless.
Installing Windows is equally straightforward. Parallels can download and install the ARM version of Windows 11 for Apple Silicon Macs, although you’ll still need to purchase a Windows 11 Pro or Enterprise licence. It also offers limited support for running older Intel (x86) versions of Windows on M-series Macs, but performance is slower and there are restrictions, including an 8GB memory limit and no sound support.
Performance is excellent on Apple Silicon, making Parallels ideal for productivity software, development, testing and many creative applications. Features such as snapshots, cloning and Rollback mode – which restores a virtual machine to its original state after a restart – are particularly useful for developers experimenting with new software.
Parallels receives regular updates alongside new macOS releases. The latest version supports macOS Tahoe and Windows 11 25H2, while recent releases have added AI-focused developer tools, including the Parallels AI Package for creating AI-ready virtual machines.
The main downside is cost. Parallels is subscription-based for most users, and Windows requires a separate licence. Virtual machines are also memory-intensive, so Macs with 16GB of RAM or more provide the best experience.
Combining outstanding performance, polished macOS integration and powerful developer features, Parallels Desktop remains the best virtualization software for most Mac users especially software developers.

Cons
VMware doesn’t update Fusion as regularly as Parallels is updated.

For many years, VMware Fusion and Parallels Desktop competed head-to-head as the leading virtualization software for Mac, with both companies regularly updating their software with new features and performance improvements. In recent years, however, VMware has slowed development, and Fusion no longer receives the same level of attention. In fact, the software has become surprisingly difficult to find on VMware’s website since Broadcom acquired the company.
Fusion 13, released in November 2022, added support for virtualization on Apple Silicon Macs, allowing M1 and M2 users to run the Arm version of Windows. Like Parallels Desktop, Apple Silicon Macs can only virtualize Windows on Arm rather than older Intel versions of Windows. VMware initially required users to source a Windows on Arm licence themselves—a frustrating process, as Microsoft didn’t make these licences readily available to consumers.
Subsequent updates addressed some of these shortcomings. Fusion 13.5, released in October 2023, introduced DirectX 11 support for improved graphics performance and added a Get Windows option that simplified downloading and installing Windows 11 on Arm. Version 13.6 followed in September 2024 with vmcli command-line support and compatibility with newer guest operating systems, although the pace of development still lagged behind Parallels.
One of Fusion’s biggest advantages is its price. VMware first introduced a free personal edition with Fusion Player in 2020, but it now offers the full-featured Fusion Pro free for personal, home and student use. After creating a VMware account, users can download the software without paying a licence fee, making it one of the best-value virtualization solutions available.
Like Parallels, Fusion creates a virtual machine that lets you run Windows, Linux and other operating systems alongside macOS without rebooting. It supports Intel and Apple Silicon Macs, allows users to customise CPU and memory allocation, create snapshots, drag and drop files between operating systems and accelerate graphics using DirectX 11.
However, Fusion no longer matches Parallels for ease of use. Downloading the software still involves navigating Broadcom’s confusing website, and while the Get Windows feature has simplified installation, the overall setup process remains more technical than Parallels. Fusion has also dropped its Unity mode, which previously integrated Windows applications directly into the macOS desktop, and it still lacks DirectX 12 support, limiting compatibility with many modern games.
Although VMware Fusion has fallen behind its main rival in polish and new features, its strong performance and free personal licence make it an excellent choice for developers, IT professionals, students and home users who occasionally need to run Windows on a Mac. Users looking for the smoothest, most beginner-friendly experience, however, will still find Parallels Desktop the better all-round option.
You’ll need to register for a VMware account, but Fusion Pro is free to download here.

UTM Virtual Machines from Turing Software is currently sitting at no.1 on the Business section of the Mac App Store. It costs $9.99/£9.99 on the Mac App Store, but, because UTM is an open-source project, there’s also a free version–simply called UTM–available on the Turing website.
UTM can run on Macs with either Intel or Apple Silicon processors (running macOS Big Sur 11.3 or later). It provides two different options depending on the type of Mac you’re using–virtualization and emulation.
So, if you have an Intel Mac, UTM can use virtualization to create a virtual machine that runs the Intel version of Windows. And, if you have a Mac with Apple Silicon you can use virtualization to create a virtual machine that runs Windows On Arm. But, if you want to run the older Intel version of Windows on a Mac with Apple Silicon, then UTM will use emulation in order to run Window since that version isn’t designed for the Mac processors. Virtualization provides better performance, but emulation is useful if you need to run Windows apps or software that require a specific version of Windows.
Having those two options available within UTM makes it a more versatile than Parallels Desktop and VMware Fusion, which focus on virtualization rather than emulation. However, this adds complexity to UTM, and the app lacks the polished interface and ease of use of Parallels and VMware. You’ll need a basic understanding of Windows disk image files, such as ISO and VHDX, in order to download and install your copy of Windows. Don’t expect the level of step-by-step help available in Parallels Desktop.
Performance is good, though. The one weakness is that UTM doesn’t currently support 3D graphics acceleration on its Windows virtual machines, which means that you won’t be able to play most Windows games that have 3D graphics. But if you just want to run business apps or check out the new AI features in Windows, then UTM is a good, low-cost option that will appeal to developers and technical users.

CrossOver is one of the easiest ways to run Windows software on a Mac without buying or installing Windows itself. Built on the open-source WINE compatibility layer, it translates Windows API calls into macOS equivalents, allowing many Windows apps and games to run natively rather than through a virtual machine.
Unlike Parallels Desktop or VMware Fusion, CrossOver doesn’t require a Windows licence, making it a lighter and more affordable option. CodeWeavers has also added a polished interface, technical support and installation tools that make it far easier to use than WINE itself.
CrossOver’s biggest strength is gaming. Apple’s Game Porting Toolkit is based on CodeWeavers technology, and regular updates continue to improve compatibility with popular titles. Recent releases have added or enhanced support for games including Diablo IV, Path of Exile 2, Kingdom Come: Deliverance II, The Outer Worlds 2 and Clair Obscur: Expedition 33. It also handles many productivity applications and older Windows programs surprisingly well.
Compatibility is still its biggest limitation. Some applications work flawlessly, others have minor glitches, and some won’t run at all. Fortunately, CodeWeavers provides an online compatibility database, and the generous 14-day free trial lets you test your essential software before buying.
Performance on Apple Silicon Macs remains good despite the current version relying on Apple’s Rosetta translation layer. That should improve significantly with CrossOver 27, expected in early 2027, which will run natively on Apple Silicon as Apple will retire Rosetta. The trade-off is that CrossOver 27 will drop support for Intel-based Macs, although existing users can continue using older versions.
CrossOver 26 and its subsequent 26.1 and 26.3 updates have focused on performance improvements, Wine 11.0, better graphics support through D3DMetal 3.0, interface refinements for macOS Tahoe, bug fixes and expanded game compatibility.
At $74/£60 for a one-year licence (or $494/£414 for a lifetime licence), CrossOver isn’t free, but it’s still considerably cheaper than buying Windows and virtualisation software.
CrossOver isn’t perfect, but if you want to run Windows software or games on a Mac without installing Windows, it’s one of the best and most convenient solutions available.

				
			

			

				
					

				
								
Pros

Cons

Windows 365 (which launched in July 2021) has the potential to really challenge traditional virtualization programs such as Parallels Desktop and VMware Fusion. However, at the moment, Windows 365 is still pretty expensive and is very much aimed at large corporate users, rather than the individuals and smaller businesses that tend to use Parallels and Fusion.
Microsoft describes Windows 365 as a Cloud PC, but its technical notes make it clear that Windows 365 is a form of virtual machine. The difference is that Parallels and Fusion create virtual machines that are stored locally on your Mac itself, and these virtual machines rely on your Mac’s own processor power, memory and storage to run Windows and Windows apps.
In contrast, Windows 365 creates a virtual machine that is stored up in the cloud, and runs on Microsoft’s own servers. The video image for the Windows desktop on your cloud PC is then streamed to your Mac – or any other device, such as an iPad or even another Windows PC – via your broadband connection.
This form of virtual machine can work well, as long as you have a fast enough – and always-on – Internet connection. But, as mentioned, Windows 365 is quite expensive, with prices ranging from $31/£26.40 to $66/£56.20 per month. That’s compared to $99.99/£89.99 for a full year for the home user version of Parallels Desktop, while Fusion even has a completely free version for home users and students.
Windows 365 certainly has appeal to larger businesses that want to provide a standardized cloud PC that their staff can connect to from any location that has an Internet connection – it’s ideal for hybrid working and the ‘new normal’. However, it’s too expensive for ordinary home users, students and smaller businesses, so existing users of Parallels and Fusion will probably want to stick with those apps for the time being.

How to use Windows 365 on Mac, iPad and iPhone.

Cons
Not really for beginners.

As we mentioned above, the third technology option – after Boot Camp and virtualization – is Wine, which allows you to run Windows apps without Windows itself.
Version 8 of Wine arrived at the end of January 2023, like version 7.5 of Wine, which arrived in March 2022, Wine still runs on M1 and M2 Macs via Rosetta 2. Wine 8 includes support for the latest versions of the Vulkan graphics engine and Microsoft Direct3D. It also adds support for the OCSP networking protocol.
If you don’t mind rolling up your sleeves and getting your hands a bit dirty, then Wine is an unusual but feasible option for running Windows software on your Mac.
Like VirtualBox, Wine is an open-source program that you can download for free. However, it doesn’t use conventional virtualization technology to create a virtual machine for installing Windows – in fact, Wine is the only program in this group that doesn’t even require a copy of Windows at all.
Instead, Wine acts as a kind of software middleman that translates the programming routines – called APIs – in Windows apps so that they can talk directly to macOS, without needing a full copy of Windows itself. And as you don’t need a lot of extra memory or processor power in order to run Windows, you may find that Wine can actually provide better performance than using a virtual machine (especially for games and graphics apps).
Wine also gets very regular updates from a team of dedicated developers who provide the software for free.
The downside is that Wine can be spectacularly confusing for beginners – to the point where we can only really recommend it to hobbyists who like a bit of a challenge.
CodeWeavers CrossOver for Mac is a little easier to use than Wine, despite being closely related to the software. But of course Wine is free, which is a big bonus.

				
			

			

				
					

				
								
Pros
Free for personal/educational use.
										
Cons
Very complicated, not for beginners

This open-source virtualization program is free for personal use – but it’s more at home in a corporate environment.
VirtualBox is a bit of a mixed bag. Like Parallels Desktop and VMware Fusion, it allows you to create a virtual machine that can run Windows and Windows apps from within macOS itself. You’ll need to purchase a Windows license for installation and a special version of Windows, Windows On ARM, for Apple Silicon Macs. 
If you want it for personal or educational use then VirtualBox is free. The disadvantage of open-source software is that VirtualBox isn’t as polished or easy to use as Parallels or Fusion. As the program is free, you also don’t get any technical support and the 200-page manual is designed for IT managers and developers, making even simple tasks like changing the virtual machine window resolution baffling. 
Luckily there is a busy user forum where you can ask a few questions when you need to. Which is a good thing because VirtualBox throws a lot of jargon at you and if you don’t know the difference between a virtual hard disk and a virtual machine disk then you might find it a bit tricky to get started.
Version 7.1 did introduce a new StartUp Wizard to simplify the setup process with separate ‘Basic’ and ‘Expert’ modes. However, this only partially addresses the program’s complex interface, and creating a Windows VM from a Windows 11 On ARM disk image on our M2 MacBook Pro took several attempts.
Version 7.1 also added support for Apple Silicon (aka M-series Macs). The support for Apple Silicon is limited though. VirtualBox can run Windows VMs in its own window or in ‘Seamless’ mode, where individual Windows apps run as native Mac apps. However, we found apps in Seamless mode sometimes move around on the screen, leaving odd graphical after-images. We also experienced occasional crashes when shutting down the Windows VM.
Oracle is really aiming VirtualBox at large corporations that have a proper IT department to help them out. However, business users do need to pay £49/$61 for the VirtualBox Enterprise edition, and you may need to commit to buying 100 licenses at a time, which pretty much rules it out for all but the largest businesses, or educational users who are prepared to tackle the free version.

				
			

			

				
					

				
								
Pros
Windows can run at full speed because its not being run at the same time as macOS.
										
Cons
Intel only. Absent from M-series Macs. 
You can’t run Windows and macOS at the same time.
You can’t run Windows 11.
									
Using dual-boot rather than virtualization technology, Boot Camp provides the best performance for Intel-based Macs that need to run Windows. (As we explained above, M1 or later Macs do not offer Boot Camp).
It’s important to make a distinction between Boot Camp and the virtualization programs that we look at here, such as Parallels Desktop, VMware Fusion and VirtualBox. Instead of creating a virtual machine that allows you to run Mac and Windows apps together at the same time, Boot Camp is a dual-boot system that simply allows you to boot (start) your Mac using either the native macOS or Windows (but not both at the same time).
Thanks to Boot Camp your Mac can act as a straightforward Windows PC, and devote all its processor power and memory to running Windows and your Windows apps. And, crucially, if your Mac has a decent graphics card, it can use the full power of the graphics card to help run your Windows software. That’s definitely the best option for people who need to run high-end graphics software or 3D games, as you get much better performance than when running Windows in a virtual machine.
The disadvantage of using Boot Camp is that you lose access to all your Mac apps while you’re running Windows. If you use Apple Mail for your emails then you’ll need to shut down Windows and Boot Camp, and switch back to macOS every time you want to send or receive an email. And, if truth be told, the current version of BootCamp 6.1 isn’t quite as straightforward to set up as it used to be.
Previous versions of Boot Camp did all the work for you – they would partition your hard drive, install Windows from a normal installer disk, and also install any driver software that you needed so that components such as your graphics card, keyboard and mouse all worked properly within Windows.
Boot Camp 6.1.19 (as of August 2022) can only be used to install Windows 7, Windows 8.1 or Windows 10. Windows 11 requires the host computer to have a TPM (trusted platform module) which Macs don’t have (some VM solutions, such as Parallels, can allow Macs with a T2 chip to run Windows 11). Since not all Macs will work with all versions of Windows, so before you even start to run the Boot Camp Assistant you’ll need to check the compatibility tables on Apple’s website to see which version of Windows will work on your Mac.
You can’t install Windows from an old installer disk anymore either, so you’ll either have to download a disk image file for Windows – called an ISO file – from Microsoft’s own website, or use your Windows disk to create one. Boot Camp includes driver software for setting up Windows 8 and Windows 10, but if you’re a fan of Windows 7 (which some people prefer for gaming) then you’ll have to hunt around on Apple’s website for the drivers you need and make sure you follow the correct procedure when copying them on to your Boot Camp partition.
Still, if you persevere with all that, you will eventually have Windows running at full speed on your Mac, giving you access to a wide range of Windows software and games that require more power and speed than you can get from using virtual machine technology. Just as long as you don’t have an M1 Mac…

				
		
For more advice about accessories and software for your Mac, iPad or iPhone see all our Best Picks.





How to run Windows on Mac: Apple Silicon vs Intel 
If you are still using an Intel-based Mac you can use Apple’s Boot Camp to run Windows. However, in 2020 Apple started using its own processors that are based on Arm architecture rather than the x86 architecture used by Intel. Now every Mac Apple sells has an Apple-made M-series processor. Boot Camp is not available on M-series Macs.
That doesn’t mean that M-series Macs can no longer run Windows, it just means they can’t use Boot Camp and they need the Arm version of Windows. 
If you want to run Windows on an M-series Mac. You can choose from virtualization options like Parallels Desktop and VMware Fusion, or emulation solutions like CrossOver and Wine, and even Microsoft’s Windows 365 service. You can read about all of these choices in our group test below as well as our individual reviews. 
Our top choice is Parallels Desktop, but all the others have some benefits that may suit you. For example, CrossOver doesn’t actually need a copy of Windows to run Windows apps, and there are even free options like Whisky and Wine.  
What are Apple’s Virtualization.framework tools?
Apple’s Virtualization.framework is a native macOS framework introduced by Apple that lets developers create and manage virtual machines without relying on third-party hypervisors like Parallels or VMware. Unlike Parallels Desktop, it’s not an end-user application. Instead, it’s a set of APIs that developers use to build virtualization software. 
VirtualBuddy, a free open-source app for running macOS and Linux VMs is built on Apple’s Virtualization.framework. Other similar options include Tart and OrbStack. These tools are aimed at developers rather than consumers. 
Virtualization.framework offers some advantages that developers appreciate, including: 
Native support from Apple.
Lower resource overhead. 
Integration with macOS security features
However, there are limitations compared to running Parallels and other apps. 
 FAQ 


1.
What is a Virtual Machine?
Virtualization programs such as Parallels Desktop and VMware Fusion run on the macOS, but allow you to create a Virtual Machine (or VM) that mimics the hardware of a Windows PC. This makes it possible to create a VM on your Mac and then install Windows – or another operating system, such as Linux – on the VM. This is a great solution as it allows you to run the Windows apps that you need right alongside your main Mac apps as well. The only disadvantage is that you need a pretty fast Mac with plenty of memory and storage to run Windows as a VM, since it means that your Mac is effectively running two operating systems at the same time.





2.
What is emulation?
Emulation is a process that allows individual Windows applications to run on a Mac without the need for the Windows operating system to be installed. This is achieved through emulation tools, such as Wine and CrossOver, which are typically used by technically proficient users.





3.
Do I need a Windows license?
It depends on which of those two methods you are using. If you are running Windows in a VM then you need a license in order to create a Windows VM on Macs with Apple Silicon processors, and, unfortunately, the less expensive Home edition isn’t supported. However, it is possible to use an existing Windows license if you have one and Microsoft doesn’t differentiate between Windows On Intel and Windows On Arm, see Parallel’s website here.
If you are using emulation you won’t need a copy of Windows.





4.
How can I get the Arm version of Windows
If you want to run Windows on a Mac with a M-series chip you will need the Arm version of Windows. (Although, as mentioned above, Parallels Desktop version 20.2 can run some versions of Windows that were written for Intel processors, albeit with some limitations (one being that it runs really slow).
The good news is that an Arm version of Windows does exist. Windows On Aar, aka WoA, is Microsoft’s version of Windows is designed to run on ARM chips. 
The Arm version of Windows isn’t normally licensed to individual users. Fortunately, Parallels has worked closely with Microsoft to simplify the process of creating VMs that use the ARM version of Windows. With the arrival of Parallels Desktop 18 in 2022 Parallels gained the ability to download and buy the ARM version of Windows 11 directly within Parallels itself. Microsoft even endorsed Parallels for Windows on M1 and M2 Macs, effectively authorizing Parallels Desktop 18 users to run Arm versions of Windows 11 Pro and Windows 11 Enterprise. Read our full review of Parallels Desktop for more information.
To download and buy the ARM version of Windows 11 directly within Parallels itself. All you need to do is: 
Press the button that says Get Windows 11 From Microsoft. 
Parallels will download the relevant version of Windows 11 for your Mac (if your Mac has an ARM processor then it will download the ARM version of Windows 11). 
You can then use the Microsoft Store app within your Windows VM to purchase a license or use an existing Windows 11 license if you have one. 
You can also buy a license through the Download option from the Microsoft store.





5.
How do I run the X86 version of Windows on a Mac
One option, if your Mac has an M-series chip is Parallels Desktop – version 20.2.0 – but it will run slowly.
If you are looking to run Windows on a Mac that isn’t powered by an Apple M-series chip, then you can download Windows 11 for free (as long as your Mac has the necessary specs, such as the Trusted Platform Module, to qualify for the free upgrade).
Download Windows 11 from Microsoft, free upgrade as long as you qualify.
You could take advantage of various deals for Windows 11 Pro including: 
Windows 11 Professional, $79.99 (usually $199.99).





6.
Can I run Windows 11 on a Mac using VM software?
You can run Windows 11 on a Mac using virtual machine (VM) software. This method allows you to run Windows and its applications alongside macOS without needing to reboot your computer.
If your Mac has an M-series chip it use ARM-based processors and requires the ARM version of Windows 11, officially called Windows on ARM (WoA) or Windows 11 Arm64. You cannot run the standard Intel (x86) version of Windows on these Macs through virtualization without significant performance loss via emulation. 
A popular solution for accessing Windows-exclusive software, games, or development tools on a Mac is to create a “virtual machine” on your Mac, which is software that simulates the hardware of a PC. You can then install Windows 11 on this VM. 
To run Windows 11 in a VM, your Mac needs to be powerful enough to run two operating systems simultaneously. This means having sufficient memory (RAM), storage space, and processor power. a machine with at least 16GB of RAM is recommended for a smooth experience. 





7.
Which Virtual Machine app is best for developers?
Parallels Desktop is the best choice for developers thanks to its excellent performance on Apple Silicon and Intel Macs, broad support for Windows and Linux, and features such as snapshots, cloning and seamless macOS integration. It provides a stable, efficient environment for software development, testing and debugging.
UTM and VMware Fusion are capable alternatives, with UTM appealing to open-source users and VMware Fusion suiting those already invested in VMware’s ecosystem. However, Parallels offers the strongest overall balance of speed, ease of use and developer-focused features for everyday cross-platform workflows.

title: PlasmaSolve bought by Apple to help make thin & durable device enclosures
content:
Czech company PlasmaSolve has been acquired by Apple, likely for its software that helps optimize manufacturing of scratch-resistant metallic coatings.


PlasmaSolve's main product was a plasma technology simulator called MatSight, which has been removed from sale since Apple acquired the company - image credit: PlasmaSolve
Apple already uses PVD (physical vapor deposition) in its existing coating processes for devices, but it is aiming to refine and develop this through acquiring PlasmaSolve. PlasmaSolve was founded in 2016 by Adam Obrusnik, and  makes a simulation software package called MatSight.
MatSight models PVD and PECVD (plasma-enhanced chemical vapor deposition) to improve process designs.
