title: Secure your digital life across all your Apple devices
content:
Macworld


One of the things most of us love best about being in the Apple ecosystem is how easily we can move between our devices with our data always available. No matter if we’re on our iPhone, iPad or Mac, the continuity of experience is one that makes us feel at home. This also means that it’s important that our digital security covers all formats and works on all of them at the same time. So, how can we be sure that connections to networks remain private and our identities are protected whichever device we’re using? Surfshark has the solution.
The internet with no one watching
With so much of our lives now being conducted online, there’s never been more need to ensure that no-one can see what you’re doing or the sites you’re visiting. Advertising trackers are constantly trying to follow you around the web, to build profiles which enable them to sell you more things. Hackers are always looking for ways to inject malware or viruses onto your system so they can steal your data, plus there’s the background threat of governments and authorities wanting to know who you’re talking to and what it’s about. One effective weapon against these invasions of privacy is Surfshark VPN.

				
					

				
			
Surfshark




Rather than leaving your communications with online servers open and easily readable, Surfshark VPN creates an encrypted ‘tunnel’ that protects any data passing through. This means that even if spying eyes manage to get hold of your communiques, they won’t be able to read them as the encryption will make them incoherent. It also has a MultiHop feature that acts as essentially a double-VPN for additional security, plus a rotating IP address to prevent profiling and Kill Switch that automatically ends your online session if the VPN becomes unavailable.
So, you can use your Mac at the coffee shop or your iPhone at the airport, connecting to public Wi-Fi networks without worrying about your data or identity being compromised.
Surfshark VPN uses industry-leading AES-256-GCM and ChaCha20 encryption, alongside the latest VPN protocols, such as WireGuard, OpenVPN and IKEv2 to keep your data secure. It also employs its own proprietary Dausos protocol, which uses AEGIS-256X2 encryption to defend against the growing threat of powerful Quantum-computer attacks, all while delivering speeds up to 15% faster than other industry-standard protocols.

				
					

				
			
Surfshark




Even Surfshark can’t see your data, thanks to its no-logs policy which is audited by the third-party company Deloitte. This means it doesn’t store or access your information or web activity, and its 4,500+ RAM-only servers (located in 100 countries across the world) wipe all data when they reboot. It’s how the internet should be: private and secure.
Best of all, Surfshark can be used simultaneously on an unlimited number of devices, rather than the 5 or 10 that other services offer, so you can stay safe no matter what you’re using and your family can even use the same subscription.
A cleaner and safer online experience
Surfshark offers more than a VPN, as its various plans (Starter, One, and One+) come with extra security features to improve the safety and quality of your online life. The Clean Web ad blocker does exactly that, stopping annoying pop-ups, banners and other intrusive messaging that get in your way and slows down your connection. There’s also antivirus protection that makes sure no-one can use your webcam without you knowing or load malware onto your system.

				
					

				
			
Surfshark




With so many data leaks being reported these days, Surfshark Alert monitors the web to see if your account or credit card details have been exposed, then warns you so you can prevent disaster. One way to stop this happening in the first place is to use Alternative ID, a feature in the Surfshark suite that allows you to create temporary online personas for signing up to services or sites, so your actual details are never given out and therefore can’t be stolen.
Such is the commitment to your privacy that Surfshark even offers up to $1milion in reimbursement for any expenses incurred should your identity be stolen. It also partners with data specialist Incogni to ensure you get your details removed from any data broker servers who would sell it on to interested parties.
Protect your data, identity and bank balance with Surfshark
As you can see, there are many reasons to sign up to Surfshark: privacy, security, and the freedom to use all your devices with the same levels of protection. But another compelling incentive is the current promotion that means you can get a two-year plan that starts at only $2.49 per month, plus Surfshark will throw in an extra 3-months for free! That’s 27 months of online safety and anonymity with up to 85% off the normal cost of the plan. In these times when prices everywhere else only seem to be going up, it’s good to know that someone has your back.

title: 20th Anniversary iPhone Coming Next Year With These 10 Features
content:
Apple's 20th anniversary iPhone is expected to arrive in the fall of 2027 with the most significant redesign the device has seen since the iPhone X.


The first iPhone was announced in January 2007 and went on sale that June, meaning the device's 20th anniversary technically falls on June 29, 2027. Apple rarely launches new high-end iPhones outside of its September timeframe, and the anniversary models are still expected to arrive in the fall of that year, just as the iPhone X did in 2017 despite marking the 10th anniversary of a device that launched in June.

all-glass design, new display technology, and a series of upgrades Apple has been working toward for several generations. Much as the iPhone X set the template for the years of iPhones that followed, the anniversary model is likely to define the device's design direction for some time.

Apple could skip the name "iPhone 19" in the same way it skipped "iPhone 9" ahead of the iPhone X in 2017, with rumors so far variably referring to the device as the "iPhone 20" and the "iPhone XX." Here is everything that has been rumored for the device so far:


Curved all-glass design with edge-to-edge display: Apple is reportedly aiming for a new design with curved glass generously wrapping around the front and back, described by Bloomberg's Mark Gurman as a curved iPhone without cutouts in the display. Facilities in Apple's supply chain have reportedly finished renovations ahead of production, with manufacturing quality said to be around that of the first-generation iPhone Air. The panel is said to curve down around all four edges for a borderless effect, going beyond the curved displays used by other manufacturers. Rather than the aggressively curved "waterfall" edges seen on some Samsung panels, Apple is said to be seeking an equal-depth quad-curved design with very shallow "micro-curves," which could make edge swipes feel more natural and reduce distortion of on-screen content. Bending the display circuitry around every edge reportedly requires an ultra-thin film encapsulation layer to protect the OLED panel from moisture and air, and one leak claims a bezel of 1.1mm, compared to approximately 1.44mm on the iPhone 17 Pro.

More advanced display: Apple is reported to be adopting a Samsung-made panel using Color Filter on Encapsulation, which removes the polarizing film and applies the color filter directly onto the encapsulation layer. The technique reduces the thickness of the display stack and lets more light through, improving brightness while reducing power draw, and the panel is said to be paired with next-generation 16nm display driver chips. Apple is also said to be employing a crater-shaped light diffusion layer designed to even out brightness so the display appears uniformly lit across all areas, including at the curved edges.

Under-display Face ID: Apple reportedly wants to move the Face ID system beneath the panel, using a "spliced micro-transparent glass" window that allows infrared sensors to pass through the display. The technology is expected to debut on iPhone 18 Pro models first, but DSCC's Ross Young has said it is unlikely to be fully ready even for 2027, and expects an iPhone 18 Pro-style smaller Dynamic Island to remain.

Two size options: Unlike the iPhone X, which launched in a single 5.8-inch size, Apple is planning two anniversary models roughly matching the iPhone 18 Pro and Pro Max at 6.3 and 6.9 inches, although the larger model could be marketed as a 7-inch device owing to its slimmer bezels and all-screen design.

Custom Apple image sensor: Apple is reported to be developing its own stacked image sensor to replace the Sony sensors used across the iPhone lineup, having already built a working prototype. The sensor is said to use LOFIC technology, allowing each pixel to store varying amounts of light and potentially reaching up to 20 stops of dynamic range.

Solid-state haptic buttons: Apple is rumored to be reviving "Project Bongo" to replace the mechanical Side button, volume buttons, Action button, and Camera Control with haptic equivalents integrated into the frame. The buttons have reportedly passed tests for use with gloves, wet hands, extreme temperatures, and with a case fitted. An ultra-low energy microprocessor is claimed to keep the solid-state buttons functional even when the handset is powered off or the battery has run out.

A21 chip: Both anniversary models are expected to use a second-generation 2-nanometer "A21" chip, shared with the second-generation foldable iPhone.

High bandwidth memory: Apple is reported to be considering mobile HBM, a form of DRAM that stacks memory chips vertically and connects them using through-silicon vias to increase signal transmission speeds. Connecting the memory to the iPhone's GPU is said to be a strong candidate for improving on-device AI performance, and Apple has reportedly discussed the plan with memory suppliers Samsung and SK Hynix, both of which expect to begin mass production after 2026.

Apple modem in the United States: Apple is aiming to have modems that outperform Qualcomm's on speed and AI functionality by 2027, following the C1 and C1X used in the iPhone 16e and ‌iPhone Air‌, and the C2 on the ‌iPhone 18 Pro‌ outside the United States only. With the 20th anniversary iPhone, an Apple-designed modem should come to the high-end devices for the first time in the United States, delivering an efficiency boost for better battery life.

Pure silicon battery: Apple is said to be pairing the new display with pure silicon battery technology for improved power efficiency, which offers higher energy density than conventional lithium-ion cells and could allow greater capacity in the same physical space. One leaker has claimed a 6,000mAh battery could come to the device, though it is unclear where that figure comes from.



mentioned by one leaker, but it is unknown whether these claims are based on supply chain information.

With the device still more than a year away, the final 20th anniversary iPhone could still change considerably from the current picture provided by rumors. A two-stage rollout has been reported for the curved panel itself, with the 2027 implementation said to introduce some distortion and brightness loss at the edges before a more advanced version follows in 2028.

title: Qualcomm Expects Apple Modem Revenue to Drop Faster Than Expected
content:
Qualcomm expects its Apple revenue to decline faster than it previously anticipated, Qualcomm CEO Cristiano Amon told Reuters in an interview following the company's earnings call for the third fiscal quarter of 2026.



Amon chalked up the loss to supply constraints, which will reduce the share of Qualcomm components used in the next iPhone launch well below its earlier 20 percent estimate. Qualcomm expects the drop in Apple revenue to start in the fourth quarter.

Qualcomm is raising its prices starting September 1 to improve its margin because of increasing costs across the supply chain. "We're just passing through big cost increases that we have," said Amon.

In fiscal 2027, Qualcomm is expecting most of its chip sales to come from categories other than smartphones, and growth in its data center business will replace the Apple-related revenue it collected in fiscal 2026.

title: Apple Says UK App Store Steering Rules Would Be 'Highly Intrusive'
content:
Apple said new UK App Store rules would give regulators a "highly intrusive" role dictating how it runs its business, reports Reuters. Apple submitted feedback to the UK's Competition and Markets Authority as it considers forcing Apple to change its ‌App Store‌ rules around steering.


The CMA wants Apple to let developers link to payment options outside of the ‌App Store‌, which the CMA says will cut fees and boost competition. Developers in the UK are not currently able to direct customers outside of the ‌App Store‌, even though that's allowed with the current U.S. ‌App Store‌ rules and the EU ‌App Store‌ rules.

UK regulators said Apple can charge developers a fee, but it must be fair and reasonable, and below existing ‌App Store‌ commissions, so developers can pass savings to customers or reinvest them in innovation.

According to Apple, the CMA's proposed rules would undermine innovation and investment, and would amount to price regulation because of the restriction on fees. Apple claims there is no evidence that allowing developers to direct users to purchase options outside the ‌App Store‌ would result in savings for customers. Apple said the ‌App Store‌ facilitated over £46.5 billion in UK billings and sales in 2025, and commissions accounted for less than 3.5 percent of the total.

Reuters.

with strategic market status (SMS) in the UK last year. Under the designation, the CMA can impose requirements meant to open up the platforms to greater competition.

content:

Like prior versions of Pastebot, Pastebot 3 records everything you copy so that it's easy to find and paste when needed. You can store links and other content that you often paste, and organize the snippets by category in Custom Pastebins.

A quick paste menu can be activated with a Shift+Command+V keyboard shortcut for bringing up your most frequently used clippings in any app, and there's a Stack function for copying multiple items and pasting them one after another.

iCloud, and there are options for customizing how many clippings are saved. You can keep up to 1,500.

title: Galaxy Z Fold8 Review: What Samsung's New Foldable Tells Us About the iPhone Ultra
content:
Samsung announced its latest foldable smartphones last week, and the lineup included the Galaxy Z Fold8, a device that's close to what we're expecting Apple's foldable "iPhone Ultra" to look like when it comes out later this year. MacRumors videographer Dan Barbera has been testing Samsung's new foldable, and the wider 4:3 display bodes well for the ‌iPhone Ultra‌.

Subscribe to the MacRumors YouTube channel for more videos.

Unlike most of Samsung's Galaxy foldables, the Z Fold8 is wider with a tablet-like look and feel when it's unfolded. It's 5.5 inches when closed and 7.6 inches when open, and those are just about the exact dimensions we've seen rumored for the ‌iPhone Ultra‌. It's not as tall or narrow as Samsung's other foldable smartphones, and it feels a lot more like using an iPad mini.

A wider unfolded display is better for using two apps side-by-side, and it's also a better screen size for watching videos. The 5.5-inch cover display is perfect for looking at notifications, responding to texts, and answering emails, and then the wider display is ideal for tasks that can use more screen real estate.

Samsung's foldable is our best look yet at what it will be like to use an ‌iPhone Ultra‌, and where the shortcomings might be. The book form factor isn't the best for vertical video, and some apps aren't designed for the screen size. Apple is working on automatic resizing for apps to match the iPad-like design, so it may be in a better position than Samsung on the software side.

iPhone 18 Pro this fall. It's also going to be missing Face ID, and going back to Touch ID on a smartphone is a big change.

Apple's design is supposed to be nearly crease-free with a sturdy hinge, and Samsung used new hinge technology for the Z Fold8 too. Samsung says the new mechanism minimizes the crease and makes it harder to feel than with prior models, but it's still clearly visible in some lighting. It'll be interesting to see how Apple's foldable compares.

Samsung didn't come out with this wide-screen foldable smartphone until after rumors suggested it was the design Apple planned to use. Samsung and Apple both have a history of adopting features after the other company comes out with something new, but Samsung seems to follow Apple more often. It looks like Apple picked the shape and details came out through leaks, leading Samsung to make a similar device. Samsung was able to make it to market before Apple because Samsung has been making foldable smartphones for years.

started around March 2018, and Samsung's first foldable came out in 2019. Samsung had seven years to pick a wider design like the one Apple is opting for, but didn't launch the form factor until a couple of months before Apple's foldable is rumored to be coming.

Samsung isn't likely to lure iPhone users away from choosing the ‌iPhone Ultra‌ when it comes out because most people tend to stick with a preferred operating system, but it could stop Galaxy users from swapping over to Apple's tablet-like design. The 4:3 iPad-like display works, and the ‌iPhone Ultra‌ is going to sell well, even at a price around $2,000. Samsung priced the Z Fold8 at $1,900, but rumors suggest Apple could charge up to $2,500.

it just launched Apple Upgrade. Apple Upgrade lets you lease a smartphone for a lower monthly price than you used to be able to get with the iPhone Upgrade Program, and it'll likely help Apple sell the new iPhone.

title: Sideloading changed everything and nothing about my iPhone
content:
Macworld


When Apple first announced that it would allow third-party app marketplaces on the iPhone, it felt like a major turning point. For years, the App Store had been the only place where iPhone users could download apps, and regulators around the world had been pushing Apple to loosen its grip on software distribution.
It was easy to imagine a future where people would browse multiple app stores, developers would offer exclusive deals, and Apple’s App Store would suddenly face real competition. Now that I’ve actually been living with alternative app marketplaces on my iPhone for the past few weeks, I can confidently say nothing has really changed.
It’s not that alternative app stores don’t work. They do. But once the novelty wears off, I found myself going right back to the App Store.
From the App Store to app marketplaces




For nearly two decades, the App Store was the only official way to install apps on an iPhone. That began to change in 2024, when Apple introduced support for third-party app marketplaces in the European Union to comply with the Digital Markets Act (DMA), legislation designed to increase competition among major tech platforms.
Rather than allowing unrestricted sideloading, Apple created a system of “app marketplaces.” These are alternative app stores developed by third parties, each capable of distributing apps that sidestep Apple’s App Store. Developers can also choose to distribute apps directly from their own websites in supported regions. Apple still maintains some oversight through a process called notarization, which scans apps for malware and basic security issues before they can run on iOS. However, developers using these alternative distribution methods are no longer required to use Apple’s App Store or its in-app payment system.

				
					

				
			
Alternative app stores are available in the EU and other regions around the world, but not in the U.S.

Foundry




Until recently, these changes were mostly limited to the European Union. Following regulatory pressure from Brazil’s competition authority (CADE), Apple expanded support for app marketplaces to Brazilian iPhone users this year. Japan is also on the list of regions where app marketplaces are available for iPhone users.
Installing another app store is easy, but there are a few hassles
Apple’s implementation is much less dramatic than the term “sideloading” might suggest. Installing an alternative app store is relatively easy, but it’s still not a fully seamless process.
Users can’t simply download apps from anywhere on the web. Instead, they first have to install an approved marketplace, which then becomes another source for downloading apps. The installation process also requires a few extra steps beyond what you might expect.

				
					

				
			
Installing third-party app stores isn’t complicated but it’s harder than just opening the App Store.

Foundry




Before installing a new marketplace, you must explicitly authorize the download in the Settings app. (This process is no longer required in the EU due to local legislation, but it’s still required in Brazil and Japan.) Once the store installs on your iPhone, it behaves much like any other app.
For those who are already familiar with advanced settings on iOS, this process is quite simple. But for others, the fact that it requires an extra confirmation step is enough to make them think twice before installing an alternative app marketplace.
What’s so great about alternative app marketplaces?
One of the biggest complaints about Apple’s App Store is how strict it is when it comes to its guidelines, putting a lot of restrictions on what developers can do. And since the App Store was the only way to distribute iPhone apps, there wasn’t any other official way to distribute apps that don’t follow Apple’s rules.
For example, the App Store banned emulator apps for years. And although Apple now allows them, there are other categories that are still off-limits, including violent games, adult-themed content, and torrent clients. In theory, alternative app marketplaces solve this problem and let these apps in.

				
					

				
			
Apps downloaded outside the App Store often offer beter discounts deals on in-app purchases.

Foundry




Alternative app marketplaces also make it easier for developers to adopt their own business models, rather than relying on the App Store’s in-app purchase system. That was the reason Fortnite left the App Store years ago, and the impetus for many of the rules in place. As such, Epic now has its own marketplace available on iOS.
For my testing, I primarily used AltStore PAL and Aptoide, two of the best-known alternative marketplaces currently available. To be honest, there aren’t many other options besides these.
AltStore is probably the most popular app marketplace for iOS, since it already existed on jailbroken devices before all these changes. It was created by Riley Testut, the developer behind the well-known Delta game emulator. In addition to Testut’s own apps, AltStore also offers some apps from third-party developers.
There are streaming apps, torrent clients, and a few dozen other indie apps like a clipboard manager that you won’t find in the App Store. Fortnite and other titles from Epic are also available on AltStore, so gamers have a great reason to like alternative app marketplaces.

				
					

				
			
Apps downloaded through third-party stores have fewer restrictions than Apple’s App Store.

Foundry




Apptoide focuses more on games. Although many of the titles available there can also be found on the App Store, the versions on this alternative app marketplace often offer discounts on in-app purchases.
Installing apps from these marketplaces is quite easy and very similar to the App Store. Of course, the entire process of updates and purchases is managed through these stores, so you won’t see any related purchases in the App Store settings.
The App Store already has almost everything I need
After the initial excitement of trying something new, I realized I had no real reason to keep opening these alternative stores, and ultimately not much has changed in how I use my iPhone.
Yes, it’s nice to have the option to download apps that aren’t available on the App Store. But the thing is, the vast majority of the apps I use every day are still available exclusively there, from banking apps to social media and streaming platforms.

				
					

				
			
Even after installing a couple of third-party app marketplaces, I still went back to using the App Store.

Foundry




When I need a new app, I still automatically head over to the App Store first. Especially since these app marketplaces don’t have that many apps available. The alternative marketplaces simply haven’t given me a compelling reason to change that behavior.
Some developers may eventually offer lower prices, exclusive versions, or apps that Apple wouldn’t normally allow in the App Store. Those could become legitimate reasons to use them. But today, those examples are relatively niche. For the average iPhone user, the App Store remains the easiest and most complete place to find software.
The more I’ve talked to friends and family about alternative app marketplaces, the more I’ve realized I’m probably not alone. Many didn’t even know the feature existed. Others had heard about it but had no interest in trying it. A few asked what they were actually supposed to gain from installing another app store.

				
					

				
			
Third-party app marketplaces are fun to browse, but ultimately, the App Store is a better experience.

Foundry




It’s less of a change than you think
The ability to distribute apps outside the App Store represents one of the biggest platform changes in the iPhone’s history. It creates opportunities for developers to experiment with different business models and could eventually enable entirely new categories of apps and services.
Some marketplaces may eventually specialize in gaming, enterprise software, developer tools, or regional content. Others might compete aggressively on pricing or subscriptions.
Despite Apple’s claims that these marketplaces could potentially harm its App Store business, the reality appears to be quite different. Right now, alternative app marketplaces are clearly niche, focusing on very specific apps that are sought out only by advanced users.
They’re available if you want them, but the App Store will likely remain the first choice for the vast majority of iPhone users for a long time to come.

title: iOS 27 Lets You Hide the Messages Button Everyone Hits by Mistake
content:
If you accidentally press the dictation or voice icon after sending a text in Messages, your music may pause while your iPhone starts listening. It's a small annoyance, but a frequent one, since the dictation/audio icon sits so close to the send arrow that stray taps are almost inevitable. In iOS 27 and iPadOS 27, Apple has finally given you a way to get rid of it.


The issue is one that popstar Justin Bieber publicly complained about, claiming that the send button shouldn't have multiple functions so close together. The post went viral, and in iOS 27, Apple has done something about it.

Quite simply, the message text field now has a new setting. You can choose whether it displays the audio waveform icon for recording a voice message, the microphone icon for dictation, or nothing at all. Here's how to find it:

  
Open the Settings app on your iPhone or iPad.

  
Tap Apps at the bottom of the list.

  
Tap Messages.

  
Tap Show in Text Field.

  
Choose one of the three options: Record Audio, Start Dictation, or None.

If you keep tapping the text field icon by mistake, you'll want to choose None.

Audio. If it's dictation you sometimes use, you'll find the microphone key at the bottom right of the iOS keyboard (if it's not there, go to Settings ➝ General ➝ Keyboard and turn on Enable Dictation.)

title: Apple Upgrade is a really great deal for one reason
content: Apple Upgrade launched yesterday, a new leasing program for iPhone, iPad, Mac, and Apple Watch (pricing here). The program has garnered some skepticism, but there’s one key reason I think it’s a great deal for users.
creator: Ryan Christoffel

title: Apple's New Upgrade Program: Is It Worth It?
content:
With the new Apple Upgrade program in the U.S., you can now lease an iPhone, but is it worth it? The answer is more complicated than a simple yes or no.


We'll use the iPhone 17 Pro with 256GB of storage on a one-year lease as an example. In the U.S., the device costs $1,099 upfront, but through Apple Upgrade you can lease it for $45.99/month for 12 months.


  
Return your iPhone.

  
Return your iPhone and upgrade to a newer iPhone.

  
Buy the iPhone outright by paying an amount equal to the device's retail price minus any lease payments made.

We dive into each of those options below.

Options

Returning the iPhone

If you return the iPhone 17 Pro and simply move on from the Apple Upgrade program, then your total cost to own the device would be $551.88 after 12 months, plus sales tax if applicable. While that is less than paying $1,099 upfront, the catch is that you are no longer in possession of the device after your lease ends and cannot resell it or trade it in.

Resale value is a big factor. If you paid $1,099 upfront for the iPhone 17 Pro but resold it for say $650 through a private sale on eBay or Facebook Marketplace after 12 months, then you only spent $450 to own the device for a year, compared to $551 if you leased it through the Apple Upgrade Program for that long. But if you somehow only managed to get $500 for the device in a private sale, then you spent $600 for the device and could have saved a bit of money by opting for the Apple Upgrade program.

$551.88 is approximately 50% of the iPhone 17 Pro's price, so Apple is essentially betting that the device will retain more than 50% of its value after one year, in order to ensure that the Apple Upgrade program is profitable. Resale prices for used iPhones can vary significantly, but Apple almost certainly expects to come out ahead.

For instance, Apple's trade-in program currently offers $560 for a used iPhone 16 Pro in good condition, and that device was released nearly two years ago. Yet, Apple is effectively "giving you back" only $547.12 on a used iPhone 17 Pro after just one year ($1,099 minus $551.88), so the math unsurprisingly works in Apple's favor.

Keep in mind that the Apple Upgrade program is partly about convenience, as you do not have to deal with reselling your iPhone — not everyone likes to deal with eBay or Facebook Marketplace. That alone might sway some customers towards Apple Upgrade, even if they know there is a chance it is not the most financially optimal decision. 

Upgrading to a New iPhone

If you return the iPhone and upgrade to a newer one, the process essentially starts over.

For example, if the iPhone 18 Pro with 256GB of storage were to be offered at the same $45.99/month price, you would pay another $551.88 during the following 12 months. That would bring your total cost to $1,103.76 over two years, and you would still need to return the iPhone 18 Pro or make a final payment to keep it.

If you had purchased both the iPhone 17 Pro and iPhone 18 Pro upfront for $1,099 each, the total cost would have been $2,198. If you had managed to resell the devices for $650 each, you would have recouped $1300, lowering your final cost to $898, which would have been less than the $1,103.76 cost of leasing the devices after two years.

Of course, the resale values we have provided are purely hypothetical. There is no way of knowing what a used iPhone will be worth with certainty, but Apple has surely put a lot of research into its leasing prices to ensure that it makes a profit.

Buying the iPhone

If you opt to buy the iPhone outright at the end of your 12-month lease, by paying an amount equal to the device's retail price minus the $551.88 in lease payments made, then you simply owe the remaining $547.12 to Apple's financing partner Klarna. This brings your total cost to $1,099, which is the upfront price of the iPhone 17 Pro.

In this case, you ultimately just purchased your iPhone 17 Pro with interest-free financing by spreading out the $1,099 cost over 12 months.

Is It Worth It?

If you simply want to spend the least amount of money on iPhones over time, buying them upfront and reselling them privately is very likely the best option.

However, the Apple Upgrade program can be worth it for customers who value convenience and predictability. If you want a new iPhone every year or two and want to avoid the hassle of selling your existing iPhone through eBay or Facebook Marketplace, then the program is worth considering if the monthly payments fit into your budget.

title: HomePod rumors: All we know about HomePod mini 2, HomePod Touch & HomePad hub
content:
Macworld


Apple’s HomePod lineup could be about to undergo its biggest expansion since the original HomePod launched. Rather than simply refreshing its existing smart speakers, Apple is reportedly preparing several new smart home devices, including products that blur the line between HomePod, smart display and home hub.
The company is said to have three smart home products “very nearly ready to release,” according to Bloomberg’s Mark Gurman. However, Apple is reportedly delaying their launch until its redesigned AI-powered Siri is ready, with the new assistant expected to debut alongside the OS 27 updates later this year.
If those plans stay on track, Apple could unveil its next wave of HomePod and smart home devices shortly after iOS 27 and the upgraded Siri are released this fall.
In this guide, we round up all the latest rumours and reports about Apple’s upcoming HomePod products, including expected release dates, new hardware, Apple Intelligence features and pricing.


What are the new HomePod products?
Apple’s HomePod lineup currently consists of two models, both of which became more expensive following Apple’s June 2026 price increases. The HomePod mini now costs $129, while the 2nd-generation HomePod is priced at $349. But the real story isn’t the current speakers – it’s the next generation of smart home devices Apple is preparing.
According to multiple reports, Apple is developing several new HomePod-related products, including updated HomePod and HomePod mini models and a display-equipped smart home hub, widely referred to as the “HomePad.”
Rumored new products include the following, the names aren’t confirmed, we are using them as placeholders: 




Placeholder nameWhat is it When Likelihood 

HomePod mini 2Updated internals, faster chip, and new colors including redMid-202610/10
HomePod 3Updated internals, faster chipMid-202610/10
HomePod TouchHomePod with a built-in 6-7in touchscreenLate-20266/10
HomePadA smart display with a 6-7in screen possibly wall-mounted. To be the command centre of the home. Late-20266/10
HomeHubCombining a HomePod speaker, display, and advanced home-control features (building on HomePod Touch concept, may not be separate product)Late-20266/10
Screen mounted on robot arm Display mounted on a robotic arm (could be evolution of HomePod concept)2027 or beyond5/10
Security cameraA security camera is said to be part of Apple’s smart home roadmap2027 or beyond5/10








Why hasn’t Apple launched the new HomePod devices yet?
The biggest obstacle is Siri.
Apple’s next-generation Siri is designed to be a far more capable assistant, able to understand conversational context, personal information and on-screen content as part of Apple Intelligence. However, the chips inside today’s HomePods simply aren’t powerful enough to support these features.
The HomePod mini uses the Apple Watch S5 chip, while the 2nd-generation HomePod runs on the S7 chip. Those processors work well for music playback, HomeKit control and basic voice commands, but they lack the performance needed for Apple’s latest AI models.
As a result, Apple is widely believed to have delayed its new HomePod hardware until it can launch devices capable of delivering the full Siri AI experience. Bloomberg’s Mark Gurman reports that several smart home products are effectively ready, but are being held back until the redesigned Siri ships with the iOS 27 software updates later this year.
That means the next generation of HomePods is expected to feature significantly more powerful Apple silicon, enabling Apple Intelligence features that the current models cannot support.





HomePod mini 2
We’ll start off with the rumors about the HomePod mini 2. The HomePod mini is Apple’s smaller, more affordable smart speaker. The new model is expected to offer a new red color option, major processor upgrade and improved connectivity.

				
					

				
			
Foundry




When is the HomePod mini 2 expected to launch?
October 2026
Apple introduced the original HomePod mini in November 2020, so it is now nearly six years old and overdue for an update.
Rumours of a successor have circulated for more than a year. In January 2025, reports suggested a launch toward the end of 2025, and Bloomberg’s Mark Gurman subsequently said that new HomePod mini and Apple TV models were expected in autumn 2025. Those products never materialised.
Attention then shifted to spring 2026, with reports suggesting Apple’s new smart home devices would launch alongside its redesigned Siri. However, that timetable also slipped as Apple continued work on its AI-powered assistant.
The latest reports now point to an October 2026 launch. According to Bloomberg’s Mark Gurman, Apple has several smart home products that are nearly ready but is waiting for the redesigned Siri to ship with the OS 27 updates before introducing new hardware.
If those plans remain on schedule, the HomePod mini 2 is expected to launch alongside Apple’s broader refresh of its smart home lineup this fall, with most reports pointing to October.
What changes are coming to the HomePod mini 2?
New red color option rumored.
The current HomePod mini is available in Midnight, White, Blue, Yellow and Orange. In September 2025, Bloomberg’s Mark Gurman reported that Apple has tested additional colours for the next-generation model, including red, although it remains unclear whether any new colours will make it to the final product.
Otherwise, it is expected to retain the same compact, spherical design as the current model, with no major external changes rumoured. Instead, Apple is reportedly focusing on more powerful internal hardware, with an S9 or newer chip able to support next-generation AI-powered Siri features.
Other changes coming to HomePod mini 2
Alongside a faster processor, the HomePod mini 2 is also rumoured to include:
Apple Intelligence support, enabling the redesigned AI-powered Siri, although some features may arrive after launch if Siri development continues to slip.
Improved connectivity, including Apple’s in-house networking chip, Wi-Fi 6E and an upgraded Ultra Wideband chip.
Audio improvements, with upgraded drivers and enhanced sound processing.
Minor hardware refinements, such as a removable power cable, although this remains speculative.







HomePod 3
The larger HomePod is more expensive than the HomePod mini, delivering richer, louder audio with deeper bass and spatial audio. The next generation is expected to get a processor upgrade, improved connectivity and better sound.

				
					

				
			
Michael Brown/Foundry




When is the HomePod 3 expected to launch?
October 2026
Apple has not officially announced a third-generation HomePod, but Bloomberg’s Mark Gurman says the company is preparing several new smart home products that are being held back until its redesigned AI-powered Siri is ready. 
If those plans remain on schedule, the HomePod 3 is expected to launch alongside the HomePod mini 2 following the release of the OS 27 updates later this year. 
What changes are coming to the HomePod 3?
Unlike the HomePod mini 2, there are relatively few leaks about hardware upgrades coming to the full-size HomePod. However, it’s expected to receive the same core internal upgrades needed to support Apple’s AI ambitions.
Expected improvements include: 
More powerful chip: The current HomePod uses the S7 chip from the Apple Watch Series 7. A next-generation model is expected to adopt a significantly faster Apple silicon chip, potentially the S9 or newer, to support Apple Intelligence features.
Apple Intelligence Support: The upgraded hardware should enable Apple’s redesigned AI-powered Siri and other Apple Intelligence features, although some capabilities may arrive after launch if Siri development continues to slip.
Improved Connectivity: Rumours point to Apple’s in-house networking chip, together with Wi-Fi 6E and an upgraded Ultra Wideband chip for improved performance and smart home integration.
Audio Enhancements: Apple is also expected to refine the speaker system with upgraded drivers and audio processing.
Beyond these internal upgrades, some reports suggest Apple is experimenting with a HomePod featuring a built-in display. That device is expected to be a separate product rather than a standard HomePod 3, and we cover those rumours in the next section.







HomePod with screen
Apple has been rumored to be working on a HomePod with a screen for years, and while it hasn’t launched yet, the evidence that it’s coming is now overwhelming. Read on to find out what we know about the HomePod with Screen – perhaps called HomePod Touch – based on the latest reports.

				
					

				
			
Foundry and Apple




When will the HomePod with Screen launch? 
Possible launch: Delayed until fall-2026
Apple has been working redesigning the HomePod to include a display for some time. Back in March 2023, analyst Ming-Chi Kuo claimed Apple would “unveil a redesigned HomePod featuring a 7-inch panel.” Kuo initially expected this product to arrive in the first half of 2024, but that timeline slipped. In December 2024, he reported further delays had pushined the launch to after WWDC 2025, citing software development challenges. Then, in March 2025, Kuo suggested the device had been delayed again, due to Apple Intelligence setbacks.
Current speculation suggests a possible release in the fall of 2026, with the release slipping as the major updates to Siri and Apple’s AI platform have been further delayed. Alternatively, the HomePod Touch may gain AI related features as part of a later software update.

				
					

				
			
HomePod with display incoming?

Foundry




What will the HomePod with Screen be like?
Display size: Touchscreen 6 and 7-inches
Software: Custom touchscreen operating system running apps like Weather, Calendar, Photos, HomeKit as well as Apple Music
One of the biggest limitations of today’s HomePod is that almost every interaction relies on Siri. A built-in display would provide a more direct way to control music, manage smart home devices and access information, putting Apple’s device in direct competition with the Amazon Echo Show and Google Nest Hub.
According to current rumours, Apple’s display-equipped HomePod will feature a 6-7-inch touchscreen and run a touch-optimised version of homeOS, allowing it to function as both a smart speaker and a smart home hub. Unlike existing HomePods, it is expected to use a far more powerful A-series chip – possibly an A18 or similar – to support Apple’s redesigned AI-powered Siri and the more demanding graphical interface.
Rumoured features:
Large touchscreen: A 6-7-inch display for controlling smart home devices, viewing photos, checking the weather, following recipes and interacting with apps.
Powerful Apple silicon: An A-series chip is expected to replace the S-series processor used in current HomePods, providing the performance needed for Apple Intelligence and the touchscreen interface.
Dedicated smart home hub: Enhanced HomeKit and Matter controls, with apps including Weather, Calendar, Photos, Apple Music and Home.
Improved connectivity: Apple’s in-house networking chip, Wi-Fi 6E and an upgraded Ultra Wideband chip are all rumoured.
FaceTime camera: Reports suggest Apple may include a built-in camera for FaceTime and other video-based features.
Possible modular design: Some rumours suggest the display could magnetically dock with a full-size HomePod speaker, allowing it to be used either as a standalone smart display or as part of a higher-fidelity speaker system.
If accurate, this would represent Apple’s biggest expansion of the HomePod lineup since its debut, transforming it from a voice-first speaker into a full smart home controller.

				
					

				
			Amazon Echo Show beside the HomePod mini, 
Ben Patterson/Foundry



				





HomePad or HomeHub smart hub: Rumors & release date for smart display with robot arm
Possible launch: Late 2026 or 2027 if Siri updates are delayed
Strategy: Brand new category of products
HomePad release date 
Apple’s first-ever smart home display had been rumored to launch in the spring of 2026, but it’s been delayed due to issues with Siri, according to Bloomberg’s Mark Gurman. He claims the hardware has been ready for some time, according to anonymous sources with knowledge of the matter.
Another leaker, known as Kosutami, who has made accurate predictions in the past, posted on X on March 5 to predict: “Autumn. Home. Integrated with Pad. Now coming.” That somewhat cryptic post doesn’t necessarily refer to the HomePad, but it seems likely. 
What is the HomePad?
Apple has reportedly been exploring a broader smart home strategy for years, and the HomePad could be its most ambitious step yet.
As far back as April 2021, Mark Gurman described a high-end device combining a HomePod speaker, a touchscreen, and a camera mounted on a robotic arm that could follow the user around the room during video calls. Gurman has made various references to this over the years. 
Reports suggest Apple may be planning multiple smart home hub products, potentially split into two tiers:
Low-end smart display (J490): A stationary device with an approximately 7-inch screen, designed for wall mounting or docking. It would focus on HomeKit control and FaceTime calls.
High-end robotic hub (J595): A more advanced version featuring a display mounted on a robotic arm. This “Luxo Jr.-like” device could function as a videoconferencing system and home security tool, though it may not arrive until late 2026 or even 2027.
A revamped, AI-powered Siri is expected to be central to the experience – and its ongoing development is widely believed to be the main reason these products have yet to launch.

				
					

				
			
Imagen 3 (Gemini)




HomePad Smart Hub Design, Features & Specs
Speculation regarding the HomePad’s internal specifications and software capabilities includes:
Processing Power: Internal code suggests the device, codenamed J490, may be powered by the A18 chip, which is capable of supporting advanced Apple Intelligence features.
Operating System: The hub will likely run a version of TVos that incorporates iOS-like features. For instance, the inclusion of the “ChatKit” framework in recent software betas suggests the HomePad may support iMessage and texting, features not currently available on Apple TV or standard HomePods. 
Kitchen Integration: A new “CookingKit” framework and expanded food sections in Apple News indicate that kitchen assistance, such as searching for recipes by ingredient, could be a primary selling point.
Entertainment: Beyond home control, the device is expected to function as an entertainment hub for streaming music and video, as well as making FaceTime calls via a built-in camera.
Advanced Home Control: Code found in the iOS 26 Home app describes an “Adaptive Temperature” feature, which could allow the HomePad to offer more granular control over smart thermostats, including energy-saving optimizations based on local electricity rates.
Camera: There are suggestions that the device could combines a HomePod with a camera, or place a camera on a robot arm. This camera could also be used to recognize gestures. Some years ago a patent was filed that related to a future HomePod that could interpret 3D hand gestures. That patent describes a HomePod that can “interpret three-dimensional hand gestures as a means of controlling the device so as to execute an action or function.”







What chips will power the new HomePods?
The biggest limitation of today’s HomePods isn’t their speakers – it’s their processors. The HomePod mini still uses the Apple Watch S5 chip introduced in 2019, while the second-generation HomePod runs on the newer, but still relatively modest, S7 chip from the Apple Watch Series 7.
Those chips are powerful enough for music playback, HomeKit control and basic Siri requests, but they are not capable of running Apple’s next-generation AI features. Apple Intelligence currently requires an A17 Pro, M1 or newer chip, making it impossible to bring the full AI-powered Siri experience to the existing HomePod hardware.
That hardware gap is widely believed to be the main reason Apple has delayed its next generation of HomePods. Rather than updating Siri on the existing speakers, Apple is expected to launch new models with significantly faster processors capable of supporting Apple Intelligence.
HomePod mini 2 & HomePod 3
Bloomberg’s Mark Gurman has said the only confirmed hardware change coming to the new HomePods is a faster chip, although he has not identified which processor Apple will use. The most commonly suggested possibilities are the S9, S10 or S11 chips, but these remain speculative and have not been reported by Gurman or other major Apple analysts.
HomePod with a screen
The display-equipped HomePod is expected to require substantially more processing power than Apple’s existing smart speakers. Because it will reportedly run a touch-based operating system alongside Apple Intelligence, most analysts expect it to use an A-series processor, with an A17 Pro or A18 among the leading predictions. Apple has not confirmed the chip, and these reports remain speculative.
Whatever processors Apple ultimately chooses, the goal appears to be the same across the entire HomePod range: replacing ageing Apple Watch chips with modern Apple silicon capable of delivering the full Apple Intelligence experience.







New HomePod Prices
The prices for the HomePods increased in June 2026:
HomePod: $349/£349 (was $299/£299)
HomePod mini: $129/£129 (was $99/£99)
With Apple increasing prices in June 2026, we think that these change are like to stick for the updated versions.
However, a HomePod with a built-in screen could command a higher price. It may launch as a separate product altogether, potentially starting around $399/£399, or higher, depending on features.







Buying advice: Should you wait or buy a HomePod now? 
With prices recently rising on devices that are already underpowered our advice would be: do not buy now. 







What is on Apple’s Smart Home Roadmap
Apple’s smart-home roadmap is expected to accelerate in 2026 and beyond, as the company expands its Home ecosystem with new hardware, AI features and services designed to compete with Amazon and Google. 
Ongoing: Apple continues to lean on the Matter standard to increase device compatibility. Updates like Matter 1.5 have added support for security cameras and energy management, which Apple is expected to integrate into the Home app.
February 2026: On February 10, 2026, Apple ended support for its legacy HomeKit architecture. This transition removed the ability to use an iPad as a home hub, restricting that role to the Apple TV 4K or HomePod. 
Mid 2026: Launch of new HomePod mini 2 and HomePod 3.
Later in 2026: Apple intends to overhaul Siri. A completely redesigned, LLM-based Siri is expected to debut in early 2026 to power the new smart hubs. Previous delays in the smart home roadmap were largely attributed to Siri’s development “snags”
September 2026: iOS 27 (expected September 2026) may include AI vision recognition, allowing cameras to recognize specific users and their actions to trigger automations while maintaining privacy.
Fall 2026: Launch of Apple’s HomePad device(s).







Other Smart Home products coming from Apple 
Apple Security Camera: Reports indicate Apple plans to enter the security camera market with its own hardware. Code discovered in iOS 26.2 includes a new “isFirstPartyAccessory” flag, suggesting support for Apple-branded cameras and doorbells that integrate deeply with the ecosystem. 
Robotic HomeHub: A home assistant with a display mounted on a robotic arm

title: 15 iPhone accessories I can’t live without (and neither will you)
content:
Macworld


Your iPhone comes with a USB-C cable. That’s it. That’s far from enough to maximize its utility and unlock its full potential. At a time when iPhones pack professional-grade processors, cameras, magnets, and sensors, there’s a ton more out there to protect, augment, and otherwise beef up your iPhone.
Not sure where to look? Start with these 15 essential accessories every iPhone user should invest in. (The following items are listed with MSRPs, but  Amazon and other stores often offer prices lower than that.)



Fast-charging plug

				
					

				
			Belkin 3-in-1 Charging Station 
Mahmoud Itani




First things first: to actually use your iPhone, you’ll need to charge it. The USB-C cable included in its box is an excellent choice, but you’ll still need a power brick. The Anker Prime 67W GaN Wall Charger ($49.99) is one of my favorite third-party options. It is compact, has three ports, supports fast charging, and features a folding mechanism. 

Anker Prime 67W GaN Wall Charger on Amazon
If you’re more of a wireless charging kind of person, you’ll want to look into the Belkin 3-in-1 Charging Station ($139.99). It can charge your iPhone, AirPods case, and Apple Watch simultaneously without cluttering your desk with cables. It also unlocks StandBy mode on iOS, which neatly displays data and widgets of your choice.

 Belkin 3-in-1 Charging Station On Amazon
More options in our best USB-C chargers and best wireless chargers features.







Protective case
It goes without saying that you’ll need to protect your iPhone with a case, as a single drop could potentially crack its pricey glass panels. The color, design, and functionality will depend on your personal taste, but we can recommend a few reputable brands worth looking into. Head to the OtterBox, Beats, and Nomad iPhone case storefronts, where you can browse through their different options. Double-check the iPhone model to ensure compatibility before completing your purchase.

OtterBox on Amazon

Beats on Amazon

Nomad on Amazon


				





Screen protector
Like cases do for the back of your iPhone, screen protectors, particularly tempered glass ones, can help prevent cracks and scratches on your iPhone’s display. Certain designs serve additional purposes, too, like privacy variants that conceal on-screen content and matte models that minimize glare. For a high-end screen protector, you can’t go wrong with Spigen and Zagg. Ailun is also a decent brand for those aiming to spend less.

Spigen on Amazon

Zagg on Amazon

Ailun on Amazon


				





Portable power bank

				
					

				
			
Anker Zolo Magnetic Power Bank.

Mahmoud Itani





A good plug is nice, but sometimes we run out of battery while we’re away from a power source. Fortunately, iPhones support a wide range of dependable power banks with varying price points. The Baseus Magnetic Power Bank ($69.99) supports fast charging through both wired and MagSafe connections, letting you top up your iPhone’s battery however you want. Anker’s Zolo Magnetic Power Bank ($49.99) is another premium option that offers an adjustable stand. If you’re on a budget, the Ugreen Magnetic Power Bank ($49.99) offers the same 10,000mAh capacity for a fraction of the price.

Baseus Magnetic Power Bank on Amazon

Anker Zolo Magnetic Power Bank on Amazon

Ugreen Magnetic Power Bank on Amazon
More options in our best magnetic wireless power banks roundup.







Headphones
For private listening, you’ve got the fairly-priced Beats Flex Wireless Earbuds ($49), which come in fun color options and are natively supported on iOS. Want something even cheaper? You’ve got the Sony IER-EX15C Wired In-Ear Headphones ($28), which offer a basic experience for casual listeners. We also can’t help but mention the Apple AirPods Pro 3 ($249), as they’re widely considered the best earbuds for iPhone users in terms of feature sets, Apple ecosystem ties, software updates, and overall quality.

Beats Flex Wireless Earbuds on Amazon

Sony IER-EX15C Wired In-Ear Headphones on Amazon

Apple AirPods Pro 3 on Amazon


				





MagSafe wallet

				
					

				
			
Apple FineWoven Wallet with MagSafe for iPhone.

Mahmoud Itani




MagSafe’s use cases extend beyond wireless charging. Personally, I attach a wallet to my iPhone’s back, as it lets me access all sorts of cards conveniently. The ESR MagSafe Wallet ($21.99) is an excellent slim option that also doubles as a kickstand. For something more rugged, you could look into the Pelican MagSafe Wallet ($39.99). If you’d rather use an official product, you could opt for Apple’s FineWoven Wallet with MagSafe ($59), though it’s not as durable as some third-party options.

ESR MagSafe Wallet on Amazon

Pelican MagSafe Wallet on Amazon

Apple FineWoven Wallet with MagSafe on Amazon
Already stored all of your cards digitally in Apple Wallet? Check out a MagSafe grip from PopSockets instead.

PopSockets MagSafe Grip on Amazon


				





Smartphone tripod
Tripods have become essential for content creators and those looking to use their iPhones’ advanced camera features. Recording a time-lapse, for example, works best when your iPhone is steady, while Night mode will only reveal the 30-second exposure option if your iPhone’s viewfinder is fixed. Manfrotto’s Mini Tripod ($46.95) is a premium option that will work with whichever iPhone model you use. For vlogging, you may want to look into the DJI Osmo Mobile 8 Gimbal ($149).

Manfrotto Mini Tripod on Amazon

DJI Osmo Mobile 8 Gimbal on Amazon


				





Bluetooth speaker
The iPhone’s built-in speakers are okay, but they aren’t ideal for long music streaming sessions. A portable Bluetooth speaker can amplify the volume and accompany you on your outdoor adventures. The JBL Go 4 ($49.95) is my personal favorite, due to its miniature, waterproof design and immersive sound quality. For something smarter and more stable, you can opt for a HomePod, which also doubles as a HomeKit hub.

JBL Go 4 on Amazon

Apple HomePod Store on Amazon


				





Bluetooth tracker

				
					

				
			AirTags can be used to track keys, bags, and other important stuff.
Mahmoud Itani





Apple’s Find My network is arguably the most reliable of its kind, allowing you to track any item around the world. All you have to do is attach an Apple AirTag ($29), optionally using the Apple FineWoven Key Ring ($35), to the desired item. This will allow you to view its location in the Find My app. You could also opt for third-party Find My trackers, such as the Ugreen FineTrack ($25.99) if you want a built-in key ring, or Ridge Wallet Tracker Card ($39) for something slimmer.

Apple AirTag on Amazon

Apple FineWoven Key Ring

Ugreen FineTrack on Amazon

Ridge Wallet Tracker Card on Amazon
More options in our best FindMy tracker roundup.







Fitness tracker
Another wearable you may want to consider for your iPhone is a fitness tracker. The Google Fitbit Air ($99.99) is one of the best wristbands for those seeking a distraction-free experience and daily health metric collection, and it works perfectly well with an iPhone. Otherwise, go with an Apple Watch Series 11 ($299) to unlock deeper system integrations, including call and text mirroring, music playback, Find My, Apple Pay, and more.

Google Fitbit Air on Amazon

Apple Watch on Amazon


				





Car mount
Car mounts are great for safely glancing at Apple Maps when CarPlay is not an option. They also allow friends to watch you drive during casual FaceTime conversations. The Belkin MagSafe Vent Mount Pro ($32.99) is a sleek option that attaches to your iPhone using MagSafe magnets. This makes it exceptionally easy to mount and detach your device.

Belkin MagSafe Vent Mount Pro on Amazon


				





Game controller

				
					

				
			
Sony DualSense Controller.

Mahmoud Itani




With newer iPhones supporting select AAA games, a game controller can unlock a more serious gaming experience when you’re away from your favorite console or PC. iOS natively supports PlayStation, Xbox, and other MFi-certified controllers, allowing you to wirelessly connect and personalize them. I personally use the Sony DualSense Controller ($74.99), as it is one of the most trusted options, charges via USB-C, offers haptic feedback, has a long battery life, etc.

Sony DualSense Controller on Amazon


				





Security key
iPhones natively support FIDO-certified security keys, unlocking a more secure form of two-factor authentication for your Apple Account and compatible third-party services. You can secure your online accounts by requiring physical authentication using the YubiKey 5C NFC ($58). This makes it even more challenging for hackers to compromise your digital identity.

YubiKey 5C NFC on Amazon


				





Smart bulbs
Other essential iPhone accessories include HomeKit-certified products, which seamlessly pair to your Apple Home, support native controls and automations, and more. I personally rely on Nanoleaf Essentials Smart Light Bulbs ($29.99), as they’re affordable, colorful, customizable, dependable, and quite simple. If you’re going for other smart home accessories, ensure they’re compatible with HomeKit to get the best performance.

Nanoleaf Essentials Smart LightBulbs on amazon


				





Cleaning kit
Correctly cleaning your iPhone contributes to its longevity and fresh look. The iFixit Precision Cleaning Kit ($14.95) comes with around a dozen different tools designed to clean your phone’s charging port, speakers, and more. You can use the same tools to clean your iPad and MacBook, too.

iFixIt Precision Cleaning Kit on Amazon

title: WhatsApp Rolls Out Web Calling, Call Transfer Across Devices, and More
content:
WhatsApp has announced a handful of enhancements for group calling over the encrypted platform, including seamless call transfers across devices and a new web calling feature.


It's now possible to make and receive audio and video calls, including both one-on-one and group calls, directly from WhatsApp Web. The new browser-based service provides access to common features available on other devices, like screen sharing, reactions, and a dedicated Calls tab with a user's full call history.

WhatsApp says the end-to-end encrypted web service will make it easier to jump on a call without leaving your browser, and it should be especially welcomed by anyone who uses a work laptop that doesn't allow app downloads.

The latest rollout also brings Call Transfer, allowing users to move an active group call from one device to another without hanging up. 

Then there's the new Waiting Room, which appears when creating a WhatsApp call link with "Require approval to join" enabled. Participants now enter the waiting room first until the host is ready to let them in. 

Two last additions round out this update: QuickHD allows users to enjoy high-definition video immediately in the very first few seconds of the call, while Noise Suppression removes background noise so that voices come through more clearly, even in loud or busy environments.

title: Best iPhone 17 cases for iPhone 17, 17 Pro & 17 Pro Max, 17e and Air
content:
Macworld


Before you even start the setup on your iPhone 17—be it an iPhone 17, 17e or Air, 17 Pro or 17 Pro Max— you should consider what type of case you need to protect it in. However good Apple’s new Ceramic Shield 2 shell is, it won’t be up to protecting your phone if dropped or scraped. A case just makes sense—and can look fantastic, too. Some are even ultra glamorous.
Cases come in more shapes and sizes and with more functionality than you’d believe. Hit these links to jump straight to our recommendations, reviews and tests to find the perfect case for your iPhone 17, 17e, 17 Pro and 17 Pro Max and Air. Or read on for more case advice before reaching the product charts. Cases for the most recent iPhone 17e have started to appear (keep reading) and we’ll add more here when they arrive.
Best clear iPhone 17 cases
Best stylish iPhone 17 cases
Best protective cases for iPhone 17
Best leather and leather-alternative iPhone 17 cases
Best iPhone 17 cases with wallet
Best iPhone 17 battery cases
Best iPhone bags
Best iPhone 17 camera grip cases
Do I need an iPhone case for iPhone 17?
You may have heard that Apple’s new-generation Ceramic Shield 2 front cover promises 3x better scratch resistance, and for the Pro and Pro Max models Ceramic Shield also protects the back of iPhone, delivering 4x better resistance to cracks than the back glass on previous models. Does that mean that you no longer need a case? A case will keep your iPhone looking at it’s best, which will be a benefit when and if you come to sell it. Also, note that neither the plain iPhone 17 nor Air feature the same level of back protection.
Do I need an iPhone case for iPhone Air?
The iPhone Air is so thin it seems a shame to bulk it up in a protective case. It’s also tough at resisting bending but it is still just as vulnerable to drops and everyday dings. Most cases reviewed here have a variant for the iPhone Air but there are especially thin cases such as the super-slim Thinborne iPhone 17 Case and Pitaka Ultra-Slim Case, or consider the Nomad Magnetic Leather Back that misses the sides altogether and protects just the back.
Why you need an iPhone case
The primary function of a phone case is to protect your high-cost but fragile device from physical damage—caused by accidental impacts such as shocks from drops and scrapes that can leave your phone with a cracked screen, scratches, dents, a shattered back or internal harm. In fact, research shows that within 10 weeks of purchase, half of all new phone users will drop their handset. D’oh!
Just being pulled from your pocket many times a day causes gradual wear that adds to the unseen damage from UV exposure and other environmental factors. Environmental protection safeguards against water and dust damage that can degrade or destroy your precious phone. Putting your iPhone into a case doesn’t make it indestructible, but it will reduce the risk of everyday or unexpected damage that might otherwise save a costly repair or full replacement. 
Which type of iPhone case to choose
As nice as Apple makes its phones look there are only a handful of colors, so a case also offers aesthetic personalization through design (there are thousands to choose from) and customized style. Love the Cosmic Orange iPhone Pro but want to save money with the basic iPhone 17 model? Why not just buy a bold orange case for the 17, such as the Beats iPhone 17 Rugged Case in Sierra Orange?
Choosing the right case material (be that silicone, leather, Graphene or Kevlar) is also key—depending on whether you are after better grip, more robust protection or luxurious leather.
Cases can also add functionality, with handy features such as stands for hands-free viewing or wallet holders for carrying cards and cash. If you ever wirelessly charge your phone, make sure the case is MagSafe compatible—most are these days.
Best clear iPhone cases for iPhone 17, 17e, Air, 17 Pro and 17 Pro Max
If covering up Apple’s iPhone offends your inner Jony Ive, look for a clear, transparent case that keeps the iPhone’s looks as wonderful as they were straight out of the box. Why pick out a Sky Blue iPhone Air or Cosmic Orange iPhone 17 Pro Max, only to cover it up in a black plastic case or something with badly drawn flowers on it? With a Clear case, you get decent protection without ruining the look of the phone—although Apple has rather mucked this up with its own version; see review below.
If you want a plain black case or flowery pattern instead of Apple’s small palette of colors, we have plenty for you to choose from further down this feature.

This simple, rigid iPhone 17 protective case from Apple is thin and light. By design, clear cases shouldn’t disguise the color of your iPhone that you chose when you purchased it. 
The Apple Clear Case is made from a blend of optically clear polycarbonate and other flexible materials, with a scratch-resistant coating on both the inside and outside. While it’s more protective than silicone cases and features a robust-looking 2mm camera lip, you can find tougher cases, which we have reviewed below.
While the Clear Case for the basic iPhone 17 is as you’d expect, Apple has somewhat ruined the idea of a “clear” case for its Pro and Pro Mac versions of the iPhone 17, which feature a slab of white plastic at the back under the camera area. It’s white whatever color of iPhone 17 Pro or Max that you own.
This is because Apple added its second-generation Ceramic Shield glass as a separate panel on the back of the Pro models—it’s on only the front of all the 17 family. To keep the back design visually balanced, the Apple logo was repositioned slightly lower. The white slab on Apple’s clear case is related to this adjustment and the alignment of the MagSafe magnets. Customers are already complaining that Apple should have created cases with a block in the color of the phone. If your iPhone 17 Pro or Pro Max is orange or deep blue that slab of white is, well I’ll say it, ugly.
The bottom of the Clear Case is nearly fully open, which reduces the level protection.
For the iPhone Air Apple has another not really clear solution: the iPhone Air Bumper. This protects the edges of the phone and matches the Air’s color but leaves the back exposed. With a raised bezel it will also stop the screen touching the surface when laid flat. You can choose the bumper color to match your iPhone Air or select another color if you are feeling adventurous. 
Apple also sells the iPhone Air Case with MagSafe in Frost or Shadow, with a 0.9mm back panel that’s reinforced with a polycarbonate frame. The inside is lightly frosted, while the exterior is finished to a high gloss. 
At 29g it’s super light, and while the rigid case adds a little bulk, it’s worth a little compromise for that layer of protection. All materials and coatings are optimized to prevent yellowing over time.
There are also cheaper clear cases, which we have also tested for you. But the Apple badge is a sure sign of quality, as you’d expect.

How to choose a case for your iPhone 17
Protection
The most common results of drops and knocks cause cracked and scratched screens, followed by chipped corners and sides. Even a basic phone case offers some protection against such everyday drops and knocks, and some are built to withstand more catastrophic accidents. Modern materials mean that protective cases are relatively slim and light. Clever design and tough-but-thin materials such as Kevlar and Graphene are key to the levels of robustness—but it remains the case that the bulkier the case, the more protection it will likely offer as long as it is also clever and made of the right stuff.
Let’s face it the iPhone is basically made front and back of glass—even if it is a new version of Ceramic Shield that Apple claims is three to four times tougher than any smartphone glass—and glass dropped on the floor usually ends in tears.
Look for raised edges (known as a bezel) around the screen that will protect it from drop cracks and scratches—it lands on these edges and not the fragile screen. Another point of obvious weakness is the camera lens area, and you should go for a case with a raised edge around that part, too, in case the phone lands that side down. Where we have the exact dimensions, we have included this information in our case reviews below.
Look for button covers—in metal or plastic. Some cases prefer cutouts but may offer less protection as a result. The Camera Control on the right side of all the iPhone 17 models is capacitive so it can’t be covered using standard materials in the same way as the other iPhone buttons can. Instead the best utilize a piece of sapphire crystal coupled with a conductive layer to communicate finger movements—including taps, slides and swipes—to the button below.
Style
If you want to keep the original Apple colors while still protecting the phone, choose a clear case. If you want to add more personality—if only to distinguish your iPhone from those of your family and friends—there are thousands of designs to choose from. Some are quite beautiful, some fine art, and some I wouldn’t want to be seen with in a dark room.
And iPhone 17 cases come in many forms: wallet cases, cases that support bike and car mounts, phone pouches, sleeves, slings and cases with belt-clips. Here we keep adding the best we can find as they come in for testing.
Fit
Ensure you choose the right case for your exact model so that it fits correctly over the buttons and camera lenses for uninterrupted use. Where possible we have linked to the buying pages for each model: iPhone 17e (6.1 inch), iPhone 17 (6.3 inch), Air (6.5 inch), iPhone 17 Pro (6.3 inch) and iPhone 17 Pro Max (6.9 inch).
Don’t think you can squeeze your new 17 model iPhone into a case for an older model. Sometimes a new iPhone is the same size as the previous model, but not the 17 unfortunately, which also has a whole new camera section at the top. Upgraders need a new case. That said, I have used an iPhone 17 Pro case on my iPhone 16 Pro. The buttons work but the flashlight is covered on some cases.
Magnetic wireless charging
Also make sure that the case is MagSafe compatible so that you can charge wirelessly with a MagSafe charger while your iPhone 17 stays in its case. So-called “clear” cases sadly require a huge white ring on their back to be compatible with MagSafe charging. Colored, patterned or leather cases hide their magnets better.
On the 17 Pro and 17 Pro Max Apple has placed its logo further down the back so the circle of magnets would cut through it. On its own clear case Apple tries to not spoil its logo or reduce the number of magnets and ends up with an ugly solution for the 17 Pro and Pro Max clear cases. Third-party clear case manufacturers have decided to remove a few magnets to allow the logo to show, and claim this doesn’t affect the magnetic fit.
You can, of course, still charge via a USB-C cable—which will always be the fastest way to charge an iPhone—and an iPhone charger.
Will the iPhone 16 Pro fit an iPhone 17 Pro case and vice versa?
If you still own an iPhone 16 Pro and fancy one of the iPhone 17 Pro cases reviewed here, you might be in luck. Our test iPhone 16 Pro fit most of the iPhone 17 Pro cases here, although some may cover the 16 Pro’s flashlight. It’s not the case the other way round as an iPhone 16 Pro case will cover the 17 Pro’s Flash and the LiDAR Scanner that uses lasers to measure distances and create a 3D map of the environment.
You can’t swap iPhone 16 and 17 cases on models other than the Pro due to size and cutout differences.
